Exam Details

The NASCLA Accredited Trade Examination for Electrical Contractors is intended for individuals performing, supervising, or qualifying electrical contracting work. It evaluates knowledge related to the installation, maintenance, repair, management, and safe operation of electrical systems in accordance with applicable codes and standards.

The examination contains 100 scored questions. Candidates must answer at least 75 scored questions correctly to meet the minimum passing standard. The examination allows 270 minutes, which provides four hours and thirty minutes to complete the test.

Ten additional non-scored experimental questions may also be administered. These questions are used for future examination development and do not count toward the final score.

The examination content includes the following major areas:

  • Project Design and Management: Planning, coordination, project delivery, schedules, stakeholders, risk, quality, and contractor responsibilities.
  • Safety: Construction safety, general-industry safety, electrical hazards, protective equipment, and electrical safety-related work practices.
  • Electrical Theory and Principles: Voltage, current, resistance, power, circuits, motors, transformers, formulas, and calculations.
  • General Code Requirements: NEC organization, definitions, general installation rules, and code interpretation.
  • Wiring and Protection: Branch circuits, feeders, services, grounding, bonding, conductors, and overcurrent protection.
  • Wiring Methods and Materials: Raceways, cables, boxes, fittings, conductor installation, support, and permitted uses.
  • Equipment for General Use: Motors, transformers, appliances, luminaires, switches, receptacles, and other electrical equipment.
  • Special Occupancies, Equipment, and Conditions: Requirements for specialized locations, systems, and installations.
  • Communication Systems: Code requirements affecting applicable communication circuits and systems.

General code requirements, wiring and protection, wiring methods and materials, and equipment for general use represent a substantial portion of the contractor examination. Candidates should dedicate meaningful study time to these subjects while continuing to prepare for project management, safety, theory, energy requirements, and specialized electrical installations.

A physical diagram or blueprint packet may be provided at the testing center. Candidates should be prepared to interpret plans, specifications, equipment schedules, symbols, conductor information, notes, and project requirements. Open Book Test

Approved reference materials may be highlighted, underlined, and indexed. Permanent tabs may be used to identify major chapters, articles, tables, and frequently referenced sections. Temporary tabs, removable notes, handwritten study notes, loose sheets, and attached additional papers are not permitted.

The open-book format places significant importance on reference familiarity. Candidates may need to move between the National Electrical Code, OSHA regulations, NFPA 70E, the energy standard, project-management guidance, contractor business material, field references, and electrical theory content during the same testing session.

A productive preparation method begins with learning the purpose and organization of each publication. Candidates should know which book is most likely to address a particular question before beginning to search. This reduces wasted time and helps create a more controlled examination strategy.

For the National Electrical Code, practice using the index, table of contents, definitions, chapters, articles, tables, exceptions, informational notes, and cross-references. For project management, contractor business, and energy-standard questions, become familiar with the chapters, subject divisions, terminology, and indexes within the applicable references. Repeated practice is more useful than attempting to memorize every page.

  2. Confirm examination acceptance. Verify that the agency accepts the NASCLA Accredited Trade Examination for Electrical Contractors for the classification you are pursuing.
  3. Review eligibility requirements. Determine whether the jurisdiction requires documented electrical experience, supervisory experience, education, financial information, business registration, insurance, or a designated qualifying individual.
  4. Complete the applicable application. Submit the forms and supporting documents required for examination approval or licensing eligibility.
  5. Obtain the approved references. Purchase or otherwise obtain the listed editions before beginning intensive course study.
  6. Use the online exam prep course. Follow an organized plan for electrical code, safety, theory, project management, energy standards, business practices, calculations, and reference navigation.

Some jurisdictions issue individual master electrician or unlimited electrician licenses. Candidates should confirm the exact classification and scope of work associated with the credential they intend to obtain.

Applicants may need to document qualifying electrical work, supervisory experience, education, apprenticeship completion, financial responsibility, insurance coverage, or business registration. The B-6 classification has important scope limitations. It does not authorize the license holder to install or modify structural members, mechanical systems, fire protection systems, or other life-safety systems. Candidates should understand these limitations as part of preparing for the license and for operating within the authority of the classification.

The exam-preparation references include the International Building Code, 2012; ACI 318-14: Building Code Requirements for Structural Concrete and Commentary; and ACI 530/530.1-13: Building Code Requirements and Specification for Masonry Structures and Companion Commentaries. These are the principal code references permitted in the current B-6 trade examination room.

Additional study references include Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR Part 1926 (OSHA); Gypsum Construction Handbook, 7th Edition; Modern Masonry - Brick, Block, Stone by Clois E. Kicklighter, 10th Edition; ANSI A108/A118/A136.1:2017, American National Standard Specifications for the Installation of Ceramic Tile; Builders Guide to Floors, 1997; Setting Tile, 1995, supplied as a used reference; Handbook for Ceramic, Glass, and Stone Tile Installation, 2017; and The Contractor's Guide to Quality Concrete Construction, 4th Edition.

The study-only references are not allowed into the B-6 trade examination room. Candidates should use them to build technical understanding before test day while practicing efficient lookup skills with the code books that are allowed during the examination.

Exam Details

The Nevada B-6 Commercial Remodeling Contractor examination is administered through PSI for applicants who have received examination eligibility through the Nevada State Contractors Board.

  • Exam: Nevada B-6 Commercial Remodeling Contractor
  • Number of Questions: 80
  • Time Allowed: 3 hours
  • Minimum Passing Score: 56 correct answers
  • Testing Provider: PSI

The current examination content outline contains the following subject areas:

  • Concrete: 4 questions
  • Masonry: 4 questions
  • Metals: 3 questions
  • Carpentry: 7 questions
  • Thermal and Moisture Protection: 10 questions
  • Doors and Windows: 5 questions
  • Drywall and Finishes: 17 questions
  • Tile: 10 questions
  • Safety: 10 questions
  • Plan Reading and Estimating: 10 questions

Drywall and Finishes is the largest individual examination category with 17 questions. Candidates should devote significant preparation time to gypsum wallboard, finishing systems, assemblies, installation methods, partitions, ceilings, surface preparation, and related commercial interior finishing concepts.

Thermal and Moisture Protection, Tile, Safety, and Plan Reading and Estimating each contain 10 questions. Together, these subjects account for a large portion of the examination and should be treated as major study areas rather than secondary topics.

Tile preparation can include substrate preparation, installation methods, setting materials, grout, layout, tolerances, ceramic tile standards, and industry installation practices. The ANSI tile standards, tile installation handbook, and Setting Tile reference help support study of these subjects.

Plan Reading and Estimating preparation should include interpreting construction drawings, identifying dimensions and materials, understanding symbols and details, performing quantity calculations, and evaluating project information commonly used in commercial remodeling.

Safety also contains 10 questions. Candidates should prepare for OSHA-related construction topics involving personal protective equipment, fall protection, ladders, scaffolds, tools, electrical hazards, material handling, and other jobsite safety requirements.

Carpentry contains seven questions, while Doors and Windows contains five. Concrete and Masonry each contain four questions, and Metals contains three. Although these categories are smaller, they remain important because every correct answer contributes toward the required score of 56.

Open Book Test

The Nevada B-6 Commercial Remodeling Contractor trade examination is an open-book test, but only specific code references are approved for use inside the examination center.

The approved exam-room references are:

  • International Building Code, 2012
  • ACI 318-11 or ACI 318-14: Building Code Requirements for Structural Concrete and Commentary
  • ACI 530/530.1-11 or ACI 530/530.1-13: Building Code Requirements and Specification for Masonry Structures and Companion Commentaries

The package study list uses ACI 318-14 and ACI 530/530.1-13, both of which fall within the approved editions for the current B-6 examination.

Candidates are responsible for bringing their own approved references to the testing center. References may be highlighted, underlined, and indexed before the examination. Permanent tabs are permitted. Temporary tabs such as Post-it notes are not allowed.

Approved books may not contain candidate-added writing before or during the examination. Loose papers and additional attached materials are also prohibited. Candidates should prepare their exam-room references in advance and become comfortable navigating them before test day.

The International Building Code is especially important for commercial remodeling code questions. Candidates should practice locating provisions involving occupancy, construction types, interior finishes, means of egress, accessibility-related building provisions, fire-resistance concepts, materials, and other code topics relevant to commercial interiors.

ACI 318 supports structural concrete code knowledge, while ACI 530/530.1 supports masonry-related code requirements. Even though the B-6 scope does not authorize modifying structural members, the examination still includes concrete and masonry questions that require familiarity with applicable code concepts.

The remaining study references are not allowed into the trade examination room. These materials should therefore be used for knowledge-building and recall rather than exam-day lookup.

Licensing Steps

The Nevada State Contractors Board regulates the B-6 Commercial Remodeling classification. Applicants must satisfy the applicable experience, application, examination, financial, background, and final licensing requirements before a license can be issued.

  1. Confirm the B-6 classification. Determine that Commercial Remodeling matches the type of interior remodeling work the business intends to perform.
  2. Identify the qualifying individual. The contractor applicant must designate a person who meets the experience and examination qualifications for the B-6 classification.
  3. Document qualifying experience. Prepare work-experience documentation showing relevant commercial remodeling and construction experience within the required period.
  4. Prepare the Nevada contractor application. Submit the required business, qualifier, financial, and supporting information to the Nevada State Contractors Board.
  5. Complete applicable fingerprint and background requirements. Follow the Board's required background procedures for the individuals identified in the application.
  6. Provide required financial information. Nevada evaluates financial responsibility and uses applicable financial documentation when establishing the monetary limit for the license.
  7. Receive examination eligibility. After the Board reviews the applicant's qualifications, approved candidates may proceed with testing.
  8. Schedule the B-6 examination through PSI. Use the examination eligibility information to arrange the trade examination.
  9. Prepare for the B-6 trade examination. Study drywall and finishes, tile, safety, thermal and moisture protection, estimating, carpentry, concrete, masonry, metals, doors and windows, and approved code navigation.
  10. Complete the Contractor Management Survey requirement. Nevada contractor applicants generally must also pass the Business and Law examination unless an applicable waiver applies.
  11. Complete final licensing requirements. Satisfy the bond, financial, and other requirements established by the Nevada State Contractors Board before license issuance.

State Requirements

The Nevada B-6 Commercial Remodeling classification is limited to remodeling and improvement of interior spaces. Its scope includes qualifying commercial structures, including structures exceeding three stories and certain buildings of fewer than three stories that are connected to taller structures.

The classification specifically does not authorize a B-6 contractor to install or modify structural members, mechanical systems, fire protection systems, or other life-safety systems. Contractors must remain within the legal scope of the license and use appropriately licensed specialty contractors when work falls outside B-6 authority.

For the standard Nevada contractor licensing pathway, the qualifying individual must document a minimum of four years of relevant work experience as a journeyman, foreman, supervising employee, or contractor in the specific classification requested.

The required experience must have been obtained within the 15 years immediately preceding the filing of the application. The total documented work experience must equal at least four full years, or 1,460 days.

Nevada contractor licensing also includes financial-responsibility requirements. The Nevada State Contractors Board considers financial information when determining the monetary limit assigned to a contractor license.

A contractor bond is required before license issuance. The Board determines the bond amount as part of the approval process based on factors including the type of license, monetary limit, financial responsibility, experience, and other licensing considerations.

The Nevada contractor license is issued to the business entity, while the qualifying individual is the person who satisfies the required experience and examination qualifications and performs the duties assigned to the qualifier under Nevada contractor law.

Test Information and Study Materials

A productive Nevada B-6 study plan should reflect the exam weighting instead of giving every subject the same amount of time. Drywall and Finishes is the largest category, followed by several 10-question areas that together make up a substantial portion of the test.

Prioritize Drywall and Finishes. With 17 questions, this category deserves the largest share of focused study. Review gypsum systems, partitions, ceilings, finishing methods, installation practices, surface preparation, and commercial interior finish concepts.

Study Tile as a major category. Tile represents 10 questions. Use the ANSI standards, tile handbook, and Setting Tile to reinforce substrates, setting materials, installation methods, layout, grout, and accepted industry practices.

Prepare thoroughly for Safety. Safety also contains 10 questions. Review OSHA construction requirements for ladders, scaffolds, personal protective equipment, fall protection, tools, material handling, electrical hazards, and general workplace safety.

Practice Plan Reading and Estimating. Ten questions are dedicated to this area. Review dimensions, symbols, plans, quantities, measurements, materials, and estimating techniques associated with commercial remodeling work.

Review Thermal and Moisture Protection. This category contains 10 questions. Study materials and systems used to control water, moisture, air movement, and environmental exposure in commercial interior remodeling applications.

Build strong carpentry knowledge. Carpentry contains seven questions. Review framing, layout, materials, fasteners, doors, trim, floor systems, and common interior construction methods.

Practice code navigation with the approved books. Use the 2012 International Building Code, ACI 318-14, and ACI 530/530.1-13 regularly so their organization becomes familiar before examination day.

Use non-exam-room books for recall. The OSHA, gypsum, masonry, tile, flooring, and concrete references should be studied with the goal of understanding the material rather than locating it during testing.

Practice under timed conditions. Candidates have three hours for 80 questions. Timed practice can help develop a steady pace and improve decisions about when a code lookup is worthwhile.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the Nevada B-6 Commercial Remodeling Contractor exam open book?

Yes. The B-6 trade examination is open book, but only the approved code references may be brought into the examination room.

Which books are allowed into the Nevada B-6 exam?

The approved exam-room references include the International Building Code, 2012; ACI 318-11 or ACI 318-14; and ACI 530/530.1-11 or ACI 530/530.1-13.

Which study books are not allowed into the B-6 exam?

OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926, Gypsum Construction Handbook, Modern Masonry, the ANSI tile standards, Builders Guide to Floors, Setting Tile, Handbook for Ceramic, Glass, and Stone Tile Installation, and The Contractor's Guide to Quality Concrete Construction are study references and are not permitted in the trade exam room.

How many questions are on the Nevada B-6 examination?

The B-6 Commercial Remodeling Contractor trade examination contains 80 questions.

How much time is allowed for the B-6 exam?

Candidates have three hours to complete the 80-question trade examination.

What score is required to pass the Nevada B-6 exam?

The minimum passing score is 56 correct answers out of 80 questions.

What is the largest section of the B-6 exam?

Drywall and Finishes is the largest individual category with 17 questions.

Does the B-6 exam include tile questions?

Yes. Tile accounts for 10 questions, making it one of the major examination categories.

Does the exam include safety?

Yes. Safety accounts for 10 questions. OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926 is used for study but is not allowed into the trade examination.

What work does the Nevada B-6 classification cover?

The B-6 classification covers remodeling and improvement of qualifying commercial interior spaces. It does not authorize installation or modification of structural members, mechanical systems, fire protection systems, or other life-safety systems.

How much qualifying experience is generally required?

The standard Nevada licensing pathway requires at least four years, or 1,460 days, of qualifying experience in the requested classification within the 15 years immediately preceding the application.

Does Nevada require a Business and Law examination for B-6 applicants?

Nevada contractor applicants generally must also satisfy the Contractor Management Survey Business and Law examination requirement unless an applicable waiver applies.

Why should I practice with the International Building Code before test day?

The International Building Code is one of the approved references available during the B-6 examination. Practicing navigation in advance can help candidates locate applicable provisions more efficiently during the timed test.

How should I study the books that are not allowed into the exam?

Use the study-only references to develop understanding and recall before test day. Focus on technical concepts, terminology, installation methods, safety requirements, and trade practices that can be applied without consulting those books during the examination.

The Nevada Contractor Management Survey, commonly called the CMS examination, covers the business, legal, financial, contractual, and administrative responsibilities involved in operating as a licensed contractor in Nevada. Unlike a trade examination that focuses on a particular construction specialty, the CMS exam addresses the management knowledge contractors need to understand licensing rules, estimating, bidding, lien law, financial management, taxes, labor requirements, project management, contracts, risk management, environmental responsibilities, and safety.

The Construction Business and Law Manual for Nevada is an important preparation tool because the Contractor Management Survey is an open-book examination. Candidates should become familiar with the manual before test day and practice locating topics efficiently rather than relying on the book as a substitute for studying.

Effective preparation should combine an understanding of Nevada contractor business requirements with repeated reference navigation. Candidates who know the organization of the manual, recognize key terminology, and understand which sections relate to licensing, financial management, contracts, labor, taxes, and lien law can use their available exam time more effectively.

This exam book package is appropriate for candidates preparing for the Nevada business and law portion of contractor licensing, including applicants pursuing Class A, Class B, or Class C contractor classifications when the Contractor Management Survey examination applies to their licensing pathway.

Exam Details

The Nevada Contractor Management Survey examination is the general business and law examination used in the Nevada contractor licensing process. The Nevada State Contractors Board requires applicants subject to examination requirements to complete the applicable Contractor Management Survey and the trade examination associated with the requested license classification.

  • Exam: Nevada Contractor Management Survey
  • Common Name: CMS Examination
  • Testing Provider: PSI
  • Scored Questions: 60
  • Scored Testing Time: 120 minutes
  • Non-Scored Questions: 3
  • Additional Time for Non-Scored Questions: 6 minutes
  • Minimum Passing Score: 45 correct scored answers, or 75%

The scored portion of the Contractor Management Survey examination is divided into the following subject areas:

  • Licensing: 10 questions
  • Estimating and Bidding: 7 questions
  • Lien Law: 3 questions
  • Financial Management: 12 questions
  • Tax Laws: 5 questions
  • Labor Laws: 5 questions
  • Project Management: 3 questions
  • Contracts: 6 questions
  • Risk Management: 4 questions
  • Environmental and Safety: 5 questions

Financial Management is the largest individual content category with 12 questions. Candidates should be comfortable with fundamental contractor financial concepts, business records, financial statements, costs, cash flow, overhead, accounting-related terminology, and the financial responsibilities of operating a contracting business.

Licensing accounts for 10 questions. Candidates should understand Nevada contractor licensing requirements, responsibilities associated with a contractor license, qualifying-party concepts, license classifications, and rules affecting licensed contracting activity.

Estimating and Bidding represents seven questions. Study should include estimating principles, bid preparation, costs, overhead, labor, materials, and other considerations involved in preparing construction proposals.

Contracts accounts for six questions. Candidates should understand contract fundamentals, responsibilities of contracting parties, documentation, changes, payment considerations, and common construction contract concepts.

Tax Laws, Labor Laws, Risk Management, Environmental and Safety, Project Management, and Lien Law make up the remaining scored questions and should all receive dedicated preparation.

Open Book Test

The Nevada Contractor Management Survey examination is an open-book test. Candidates may use the Construction Business and Law Manual for Nevada during the examination.

The open-book format makes reference navigation an important part of preparation. Candidates should learn how the manual is organized, identify the major business and law sections, and practice finding information under timed conditions.

The manual should not be treated as a book that can simply be searched from beginning to end during the exam. With 60 scored questions and 120 minutes allotted to the scored portion, candidates have an average of approximately two minutes per scored question. Efficient navigation matters.

One useful approach is to first identify the subject area of the question. A question involving contractor license requirements should direct the candidate toward licensing material, while a question involving financial statements or business costs should point toward financial management. Questions involving notices, payment rights, or lien procedures should direct attention toward lien-law content.

Candidates should also become familiar with key terms used throughout construction business and law. Recognizing the correct terminology can make it much easier to locate an answer quickly in an open-book examination.

Licensing Steps

The Contractor Management Survey examination is part of the broader Nevada contractor licensing process. The exact pathway depends on the classification requested and the applicant's circumstances, but the general process includes application review, qualification, examinations when required, and completion of the remaining licensing requirements.

  1. Select the appropriate Nevada contractor classification. Determine the classification that matches the construction work the business intends to perform.
  2. Identify the qualifying individual. Designate the person whose experience and qualifications will support the contractor license application.
  3. Document qualifying experience. Prepare the applicable experience documentation required for the requested classification.
  4. Prepare the Nevada contractor license application. Gather required business information, qualifier information, financial documentation, and supporting materials.
  5. Submit the application to the Nevada State Contractors Board. The Board reviews the application and verifies the applicant's qualifications.
  6. Receive examination eligibility when testing is required. An examination eligibility notice is provided after the application has been filed and the applicable qualifications have been reviewed.
  7. Schedule the required examinations. Candidates who must test schedule the Contractor Management Survey examination and the applicable trade examination.
  8. Prepare for the CMS examination. Study the Construction Business and Law Manual for Nevada and review the licensing, financial, estimating, contract, tax, labor, lien, project management, risk management, environmental, and safety topics represented on the exam.
  9. Prepare for the applicable trade examination. Candidates should separately study the trade subjects and references associated with their requested classification.
  10. Complete the required examinations. Satisfy the applicable business and law and trade examination requirements.
  11. Complete remaining licensing requirements. Address applicable financial responsibility, bonding, background, and other requirements established by the Nevada State Contractors Board.

The Nevada State Contractors Board provides examination eligibility after an application is filed and the applicant's experience has been reviewed. Candidates should follow the instructions contained in their eligibility notice when scheduling required examinations.

State Requirements

Nevada generally requires contractor license applicants who are subject to testing to pass both a general business and law examination and the trade examination applicable to the requested classification. The Contractor Management Survey serves as the general business and law examination.

The CMS examination is relevant across contractor classifications because operating a licensed contracting business requires more than technical trade ability. Contractors must also understand licensing responsibilities, bidding, contracts, financial management, labor requirements, taxes, risk, safety, and other business obligations.

Applicants receive examination eligibility after filing their application and completing the applicable qualification review. Candidates should not treat passing the Contractor Management Survey as the final step in licensing. The CMS exam is one component of the overall contractor license process.

Depending on the application, candidates may also need to pass a trade examination specific to the requested license classification. Applicants must complete all other applicable Nevada State Contractors Board requirements before a license can be issued.

The Nevada State Contractors Board may also determine whether an applicant qualifies for an examination waiver or other licensing pathway under applicable rules. Candidates should follow the requirements that apply to their individual application and classification.

Understanding these licensing responsibilities is also part of CMS preparation. The examination tests whether candidates understand the business and regulatory framework that accompanies licensed contracting activity in Nevada.

Test Information and Study Materials

The biggest score gains usually come from tightening the same repeatable habits:

  • Stop losing points to exceptions: train yourself to look for exceptions and notes before committing to an answer.
  • Stop losing time to wandering: train the “neighborhood” method so you go directly to the right chapter/article/part.
  • Stop losing points to misreads: train yourself to slow down on wording that changes everything (“where required,” “shall not,” “maximum,” “minimum,” “nearest,” and “not less than”).
  • Stop losing points to table mistakes: train consistent table habits: read headings, confirm conditions, then read notes.

Here’s a practical way to use your 12 practice exams plus 2 full final exams like a complete prep system:

  • Step 1: Take a diagnostic exam. Use Practice Exam 1 timed. Don’t pause mid-exam to research. Your goal is to identify your patterns: slow lookups, rushed reading, table errors, or weak topics.

  • Step 3: Review by proving the answer in the code. For any NEC-driven miss, find the exact section/table that supports the correct answer. This builds open-book skill and confidence.
  • Step 4: Train two-pass pacing. First pass: answer what you can efficiently and move past time sinks. Second pass: return to the tougher questions with the time you protected.
  • Step 5: Rotate practice to match the blueprint. Make sure your practice includes wiring methods/materials, branch circuits/conductors, equipment/devices, services, and special occupancies—because those areas carry the biggest weight.
  • Step 6: Use the two Final Exams as simulations. Take them near the end of your prep, timed, in a quiet setting, with minimal interruptions. Review carefully afterward—your best improvements often come after a full simulation.

The Nevada Business Contractor Management Survey Exam Prep Study Flash Cards set includes 198 flash cards for candidates preparing for Nevada’s required Business and Law examination, commonly referred to as the Contractor Management Survey or CMS exam.

Becoming a licensed contractor in Nevada requires more than knowing how to perform construction work. Qualifying individuals also need an understanding of the laws, business practices, financial responsibilities, contracts, employment requirements, project-management principles, and licensing rules that apply to contractors operating in Nevada. The Contractor Management Survey examination is designed to evaluate this knowledge.

These 198 Nevada Contractor Management Survey exam prep flash cards provide a practical way to review that material through active recall. Included: 198 Nevada Business Contractor Management Survey Exam Prep Study Flash Cards.

Exam Details

The Nevada State Contractors Board requires qualifying individuals seeking contractor licensure to pass a general Business and Law examination known as the Contractor Management Survey or CMS, unless the applicant qualifies for an applicable examination waiver. Depending on the contractor classification being pursued, a separate trade examination may also be required.

The Nevada Contractor Management Survey examination is administered by PSI Services LLC on behalf of the Nevada State Contractors Board.

The current CMS examination contains 60 scored questions. Candidates receive 120 minutes for the scored portion of the examination.

The examination also includes 3 non-scored questions with an additional 6 minutes allotted for those items. This results in a total examination appointment time of approximately 126 minutes for the CMS questions.

The minimum passing score is 45 correct answers out of 60 scored questions, which equals 75%.

The official examination content outline divides the 60 scored questions among the following subject areas:

  • Licensing: 10 questions
  • Estimating and Bidding: 7 questions
  • Lien Law: 3 questions
  • Financial Management: 12 questions
  • Tax Laws: 5 questions
  • Labor Laws: 5 questions
  • Project Management: 3 questions
  • Contracts: 6 questions
  • Risk Management: 4 questions
  • Environmental and Safety: 5 questions

Financial Management represents the largest individual content area with 12 scored questions, followed by Licensing with 10 questions. Estimating and Bidding, Contracts, Tax Laws, Labor Laws, Environmental and Safety, Risk Management, Project Management, and Lien Law are also part of the examination.

This distribution means candidates need a balanced preparation strategy. A contractor who is comfortable estimating construction work may still need significant preparation in licensing law, financial concepts, taxes, labor requirements, contracts, or lien law. Likewise, candidates with strong business backgrounds should still become familiar with the Nevada-specific contractor requirements contained in the approved reference.

Open Book Test

The Nevada Contractor Management Survey examination is an open-book test. Candidates may use the approved Construction Business and Law Manual for Nevada during the examination.

Open-book testing makes reference navigation an important part of exam preparation. Candidates have a limited amount of testing time and should not expect to read large sections of the manual for the first time while answering questions. Becoming familiar with the organization of the book before examination day can make it easier to locate the information associated with licensing, contracts, finances, tax laws, employment requirements, lien law, and other tested subjects.

The approved reference may be highlighted, underlined, and indexed before the examination session. However, the reference may not contain written notes. Candidates also may not write in or highlight their references during the examination.

Additional loose or attached papers are not permitted with the approved reference. Permanent tabs may be used to index the book, but temporary tabs such as Post-it notes are not allowed.

Candidates may also use a silent, nonprinting, non-programmable calculator that complies with the testing requirements.

Flash cards can complement an open-book testing strategy by strengthening recognition of the material before you begin searching the manual. When you understand whether a question concerns licensing, financial management, lien law, contracts, or another specific area, you can approach the reference with a more focused search.

A useful study technique is to answer a flash card first and then locate the supporting subject in the Nevada manual. This combines recall practice with book-navigation training and helps you become increasingly familiar with where major topics are located.

Licensing Steps

The Contractor Management Survey examination is part of the Nevada contractor licensing process administered by the Nevada State Contractors Board. Candidates must follow the state application and examination sequence before scheduling the required tests.

  1. Determine the contractor classification you are pursuing. Nevada licenses contractors according to specific classifications. The classification determines whether a separate trade examination is required in addition to the CMS examination.
  2. Submit the contractor license application to the Nevada State Contractors Board. Candidates may not schedule the licensing examinations before submitting the applicable contractor application.
  3. Complete the required experience documentation. The Nevada State Contractors Board reviews the qualifying individual’s experience as part of the application process.
  4. Receive examination eligibility. After the application is submitted and the Board verifies the applicable experience requirements, the qualifying individual receives an Examination Eligibility form and Candidate ID number.
  5. Schedule the Contractor Management Survey examination. Eligible candidates schedule their examination through PSI.
  6. Prepare for the CMS examination. Study the Construction Business and Law Manual for Nevada, review the examination content areas, and practice navigating the approved reference.
  7. Take and pass the CMS examination. Candidates must earn at least 45 correct answers out of 60 scored questions.
  8. Take the required trade examination when applicable. Nevada generally requires a trade examination specific to the contractor classification in addition to the CMS examination, unless the classification or applicant qualifies for an applicable waiver.
  9. Complete the remaining licensing requirements. Examination results are only one part of Nevada contractor licensing. Applicants must satisfy the other requirements established by the Nevada State Contractors Board.
  10. Receive approval before operating under the contractor license. Passing the examination does not by itself authorize a person or business to engage in contracting activities that require Nevada licensure.

Candidates should pay close attention to the examination authorization process. The Nevada State Contractors Board states that applicants may not schedule their required examination until the contractor application has been submitted and an Examination Eligibility form has been issued.

State Requirements

The Nevada State Contractors Board regulates contractor licensing in Nevada. The qualifying individual for a contractor license is generally required to pass the Business and Law Contractor Management Survey examination and the trade examination associated with the requested classification unless an applicable examination waiver applies.

The CMS examination is the general business and law portion of the licensing examination process. It is intended to evaluate whether a candidate understands important responsibilities associated with operating and managing a contracting business in Nevada.

Nevada’s licensing process begins with the contractor license application rather than with independent examination scheduling. The applicant submits the application to the Nevada State Contractors Board, and the Board reviews qualifying experience before issuing examination eligibility.

Once approved, the qualifying individual receives the information needed to schedule the required examination through PSI. Candidates pursuing classifications that require a trade examination will generally need to complete both the CMS and the applicable trade examination.

Nevada also establishes rules governing examination retakes. A candidate who fails an examination may reschedule after the required waiting period. The Nevada State Contractors Board states that if an examination is failed three times, the contractor license application becomes void under the applicable Nevada administrative requirements.

The Contractor Management Survey examination should therefore be treated as a significant part of the overall licensing process. Preparation should cover both the tested business principles and the Nevada-specific contractor laws and procedures identified in the approved reference.

What is the Nevada CMS exam?

Exam Details

The Nevada C-5 Concrete Contractor trade examination is administered through PSI for candidates authorized to test through the Nevada State Contractors Board.

  • Exam: Nevada C-5 Concrete Contractor
  • Testing Provider: PSI
  • Number of Questions: 60
  • Time Allowed: 2 hours
  • Minimum Passing Score: 42 correct answers

The examination is divided into the following subject areas:

  • Safety: 6 questions
  • Concrete-Earthwork: 7 questions
  • Concrete: 15 questions
  • Concrete-Reinforcement: 10 questions
  • Concrete-Formwork: 12 questions

Concrete is the largest individual category with 15 questions. Candidates should review concrete materials, placement, consolidation, finishing, curing, joints, surface preparation, quality practices, and related field procedures.

Concrete-Formwork accounts for 12 questions. Preparation should include forms, molds, slipforms, pans, supports, bracing, alignment, stripping, materials, and practical formwork considerations associated with concrete placement.

Concrete-Reinforcement contains 10 questions. Candidates should understand reinforcing steel, embedded materials, placement, cover, spacing, development concepts, and related requirements that may be found in ACI 318-14.

Concrete-Cutting also accounts for 10 questions. Candidates should prepare for sawing, cutting, drilling, coring, joint cutting, equipment use, and practical considerations associated with concrete and asphaltic paving materials.

Concrete-Earthwork represents seven questions and may involve excavation, grading, site preparation, subgrade conditions, compaction, and other earthwork relationships relevant to concrete construction.

Safety contributes six questions. Candidates should understand hazards associated with formwork, reinforcing steel, excavation, concrete placement, saw cutting, tools, personal protective equipment, and general construction operations.

  12. Complete remaining licensing requirements. Satisfy applicable bonding, financial responsibility, background, and other Nevada State Contractors Board requirements before license issuance.

The Nevada C-5 Concrete classification authorizes a contractor to prepare surfaces and place reinforcing steel and other embedded materials essential to or comprising an integral part of concrete or concrete construction.

The classification also covers pouring, placing, finishing, and installing concrete, as well as constructing and assembling forms, molds, slipforms, and pans used in concrete construction.

Additional authorized work includes applying concrete sealants and other waterproofing products and sawing, cutting, drilling, and coring concrete and asphaltic paving material.

This scope means that C-5 preparation should extend beyond basic placement and finishing. Candidates should understand the entire concrete construction process, including site preparation, reinforcement, formwork, placement, curing, finishing, waterproofing, cutting, drilling, and coring.

Test Information and Study Materials

A strong Nevada A-7 study plan should divide preparation into major categories such as excavation methods, grading, equipment, safety, trenching, site work, utility awareness, and construction planning.

Excavation methods should be reviewed in detail. Understand the differences between common excavation operations, how material is removed and transported, how site conditions affect production, and how equipment choices influence the work.

Grading should include cut-and-fill operations, establishing elevations, slopes, drainage considerations, site preparation, finish grading, and the relationship between excavation and final site conditions.

Earthmoving equipment is another major preparation area. Candidates should understand the applications of excavators, bulldozers, loaders, graders, scrapers, compactors, trucks, and other machines commonly used for excavation and grading.

Equipment questions may require you to identify which machine is most appropriate for a particular operation. Review equipment capabilities, common production methods, operating limitations, and how haul distance or site conditions can affect equipment selection.

Soils and compaction are important because excavation and grading work depends heavily on material characteristics. Study basic soil behavior, moisture, compaction methods, density considerations, backfill practices, and the relationship between soil conditions and construction performance.

Trenching deserves focused preparation. Candidates should understand excavation hazards, trench stability, protective systems, safe access, spoil placement, equipment hazards, and worker protection principles.

OSHA construction safety should be studied as practical knowledge. Since the test is closed book, review the safety principles repeatedly and use practice questions to strengthen recall of proper jobsite procedures.

Underground utilities are particularly important for excavation contractors. Road and bridge construction specifications should also be part of preparation. Earthwork frequently forms the foundation for road construction, making knowledge of excavation, embankments, grading, materials, preparation, and construction specifications valuable.

Construction planning should include sequencing work, selecting equipment, estimating production, organizing material movement, coordinating site activities, and maintaining efficient operations.

Exam Details

The Nevada C-5 Concrete Contractor trade examination is administered through PSI for candidates authorized to test through the Nevada State Contractors Board.

The examination is divided into the following subject areas:

Concrete-Earthwork accounts for seven questions and may include excavation, site preparation, grading, subgrade conditions, trenching relationships, compaction, and other earthwork considerations that affect concrete construction.

Licensing Steps

The Nevada State Contractors Board regulates the C-5 Concrete classification. Passing the C-5 trade examination is one part of the complete Nevada contractor licensing process.

  2. Identify the qualifying individual. Designate the person who will satisfy the applicable experience and examination requirements.
  3. Document qualifying experience. Prepare records showing relevant concrete work involving placement, finishing, reinforcement, formwork, excavation, cutting, drilling, coring, sealants, waterproofing, and related responsibilities.
  4. Prepare the Nevada contractor license application. Gather business information, qualifier information, experience documentation, financial information, and required supporting materials.
  5. Submit the application. The Nevada State Contractors Board reviews the applicant's qualifications before examination eligibility is established.
  6. Complete applicable background requirements. Follow required disclosure, fingerprint, and background procedures.
  7. Meet financial responsibility requirements. Provide the applicable financial information required during the licensing process.
  8. Receive examination eligibility. Candidates required to test can proceed with scheduling after authorization.
  9. Schedule the C-5 examination through PSI. Arrange the Concrete Contractor trade examination after receiving eligibility.
  10. Prepare for the trade examination. Review concrete, reinforcement, formwork, earthwork, cutting, safety, and approved-reference navigation.
  11. Complete applicable contractor management requirements. Nevada contractor licensing also includes management qualification in addition to the trade examination.
  12. Complete remaining licensing requirements. Satisfy applicable financial, bonding, background, and other Nevada State Contractors Board requirements before license issuance.

This scope explains why the examination includes subjects outside direct gas-pipe assembly. Pipeline construction starts before the pipe enters the trench and continues after the joints are completed. Equipment and Devices represents 8% and includes luminaires, receptacles, switches, appliances, and other electrical equipment. Candidates should understand both practical installation concepts and applicable code rules.

Special Occupancies, Equipment, and Conditions represents 7%. Topics include swimming pools and similar installations, low-voltage circuits, alarm systems, and similar special conditions. Although this is the smallest percentage of the exam, it remains part of the overall score and should not be ignored.

Exam Details

The Nevada General Building Contractor (B) examination is administered by PSI for the Nevada State Contractors Board. Eligibility to schedule the examination is determined by the Board after the contractor license application and supporting qualifications have been reviewed.

The B trade examination contains 80 questions. Candidates are allowed three hours to complete the exam, and the minimum passing score is 56 correct answers. The examination is administered by computer at an approved PSI testing location. A small number of additional non-scored questions may also appear during the examination and count toward the total testing time.

The official examination outline distributes questions across the following subject areas:

  • Sitework: 6 questions
  • Concrete: 12 questions
  • Masonry: 6 questions
  • Metals: 12 questions
  • Carpentry: 7 questions
  • Thermal and Moisture Protection: 9 questions
  • Doors and Windows: 4 questions
  • Drywall and Finishes: 4 questions
  • Safety: 5 questions
  • Plan Reading and Estimating: 12 questions
  • Nevada One Call: 3 questions

The examination may include questions based on the listed references, trade knowledge, and accepted construction practices. Code-related questions are based on the code editions identified for the examination. Candidates should study the applicable editions rather than relying only on a newer or older code that may contain different provisions, numbering, tables, or requirements.

The Nevada State Contractors Board generally requires applicants to pass both the applicable trade examination and the Contractor Management Survey examination unless a waiver applies. Exam eligibility is issued after the Board reviews the application and confirms that the applicant or designated trade qualified individual satisfies the applicable requirements.

Open Book Test

The Nevada General Building Contractor (B) examination is an open-book test, but only specifically approved references may be taken into the examination room. For the current B examination, the approved exam-room references are the International Building Code, the listed ACI structural concrete standard, and the listed ACI masonry standard.

Candidates are responsible for bringing their own approved books to the testing center. Approved references may be highlighted, underlined, and indexed before the examination. They may not contain written notes, added loose papers, or unauthorized attachments. Permanent tabs may be used, but temporary tabs such as removable sticky notes are not permitted.

Writing in or highlighting a reference during the examination is prohibited. Candidates should complete all permitted highlighting, underlining, and tabbing before arriving at the testing center. Preparing books in advance can make it easier to move between major chapters, locate tables, identify commonly tested subjects, and avoid losing time searching through unfamiliar material.

Although the exam is open book, success depends on knowing how the references are organized. Attempting to research every question from the beginning can consume too much time. A stronger approach is to learn the major concepts, recognize which book applies to a question, and use the approved references to confirm details or locate exact code requirements.

A silent, nonprinting, non-programmable calculator may be used in the examination center. Candidates should review the current PSI Candidate Information Bulletin before test day for identification requirements, testing-center rules, security procedures, and any updates to the approved-reference policy.

Licensing Steps

The Nevada contractor licensing process begins with an application to the Nevada State Contractors Board. The applicant must identify the requested classification, designate the appropriate qualified individual, submit the required supporting documents, and complete the Board’s review process.

  1. Determine the appropriate classification. The B classification applies to qualifying general building work involving the construction or remodeling of buildings or structures and the coordinated use of more than two unrelated building trades or crafts.
  2. Select the qualified individual. The trade qualified individual may be an owner, officer, member, manager, or bona fide employee who is actively engaged in the contracting business.
  3. Document qualifying experience. The applicant must provide the required evidence of experience in the classification being requested.
  4. Submit the contractor license application. The Nevada State Contractors Board reviews the application, experience documentation, financial information, and other required materials.
  5. Complete fingerprint requirements. Applicants must submit fingerprints for the required state and national criminal history review.
  6. Receive examination eligibility. After the Board accepts the applicant’s qualifications for testing, an eligibility notice is issued with instructions for scheduling through PSI.
  7. Schedule and take the required examinations. Candidates schedule the B trade examination and the Contractor Management Survey examination unless an examination waiver has been approved.
  8. Complete remaining licensing requirements. After the examinations and application review are completed, the Board provides instructions regarding any remaining requirements associated with license issuance.

Passing an examination does not by itself issue a Nevada contractor license. The applicant must complete the full Board application process and satisfy all requirements applicable to the business, qualified individual, requested classification, and approved monetary limit.

State Requirements

The Nevada State Contractors Board regulates contractor licensing in Nevada. Businesses and individuals performing work that falls within Nevada’s contractor licensing laws must hold the appropriate license before contracting, bidding, or performing regulated construction work.

The person serving as the trade qualified individual must generally have at least four full years of qualifying experience within the 15 years immediately preceding the application. Qualifying experience may include work as a journeyman, supervising employee, or contractor in the requested classification. Approved education or training may satisfy a portion of the experience requirement, subject to the Board’s rules and review.

The Board evaluates experience documentation to determine whether it demonstrates the depth and scope of work required for the requested classification. Applicants should provide complete information describing the type of construction performed, responsibilities held, projects completed, trades supervised, and level of decision-making authority.

The B classification is intended for general building work in which the primary purpose is the construction or remodeling of a building or structure and the project requires more than two unrelated building trades or crafts. A general building contractor acting as the prime contractor may coordinate multiple trades within the authorized scope. Specialty work outside that scope may require the appropriate specialty classification.

Nevada contractor licenses are also subject to financial responsibility requirements and a monetary limit. The monetary limit establishes the maximum value of work the contractor may undertake on one or more contracts at a single construction site or subdivision for one client. The Board determines the approved limit after reviewing the applicant’s financial information and other required materials.

Applicants should review the current Nevada State Contractors Board application materials before submitting their paperwork. Incomplete experience documentation, inconsistent business records, missing financial information, or unresolved application questions may delay the eligibility and licensing process.

Test Information and Study Materials

Effective preparation should reflect the weighting of the official exam outline. Concrete, metals, plan reading, and estimating account for a substantial portion of the examination, so candidates should dedicate adequate study time to those subjects while still reviewing every content area.

Begin by becoming familiar with the table of contents, chapter organization, index, major tables, and terminology in each approved book. A structural concrete question may require ACI 318, a masonry design question may point to ACI 530/530.1, and a building code question may require the International Building Code.

Use permanent tabs to identify major chapters and frequently referenced subjects. Keep the tabbing system simple enough to scan quickly. Too many tabs can make a book harder to navigate, while a logical system based on major exam subjects can reduce search time.

For books that cannot be taken into the examination, focus on learning the underlying principles rather than trying to memorize every sentence. Review excavation safety, steel erection procedures, gypsum construction, post-tensioning fundamentals, masonry installation, concrete quality practices, and underground utility marking requirements until you can recognize the correct field procedure or safety principle without needing the reference in front of you.

Timed practice is also important. With 80 questions and three hours, candidates must manage approximately two minutes and fifteen seconds per question. Some questions will take less time, while calculations, plan interpretation, or code searches may require longer. Practice answering familiar questions first, marking difficult questions for review, and avoiding excessive time on a single lookup.

In the testing room, you have to read carefully, apply the right requirement, and keep moving—often when multiple answers look close.

This Nevada 2023 Journeyman Electrician Exam Prep and Study Guide is built for the way journeyman exams actually feel: timed, multiple-choice, code-driven, and designed to reward electricians who can navigate the National Electrical Code efficiently. You need a plan you can stick with: short, timed practice sessions during the week, focused review on weekends, and full-length simulations when you’re close to test day.

Nevada’s Electrical Qualifications Card Program uses International Code Council (ICC) national electrician exams for journeyman and master electrical cards. Training with realistic practice exams is one of the best ways to prepare for that style of testing—because it builds the skill that matters most: fast, accurate code use under time pressure.

What You Get

  • 12 Practice Exams built to improve accuracy, strengthen NEC navigation, and train steady pacing.
  • 2 Full Final Exams for realistic exam-day simulations and confidence-building repetition.
  • Exam-style multiple-choice practice designed to reduce common misses like misreads, missed exceptions, and wrong table selections.
  • Open-book preparation focus so you practice confirming answers efficiently using your code reference.

Exam Details

Nevada’s Electrical Qualifications Card Program uses ICC national electrician examinations to obtain Nevada journeyman and master electrical cards. The program’s Nevada electrical exam information explains that ICC offers national electrician exams and that testing is available through Pearson VUE testing centers and ICC PRONTO online testing options, depending on exam availability.

ICC’s National Standard Journeyman Electrician exam outline describes a journeyman electrician exam format of:

  • 80 multiple-choice questions
  • 4-hour time limit
  • Open book

The same ICC outline also provides a clear content-area weighting that helps you study smarter (not just longer). The largest single domain is Wiring Methods and Materials, followed by Branch Circuits and Conductors, Equipment and Devices, and key NEC-heavy areas such as services and grounding/bonding.

  • General Knowledge: 6%
  • Services and Service Equipment: 11%
  • Feeders: 4%
  • Branch Circuits and Conductors: 19%
  • Wiring Methods and Materials: 26%
  • Equipment and Devices: 13%
  • Control Devices: 4%
  • Motors and Generators: 6%
  • Special Occupancies, Equipment, and Conditions: 11%

This study guide is designed to help you prepare for that reality: mixed topics, heavy NEC usage, and the need to stay accurate while you move quickly through 80 questions.

Open Book Test

Yes—this is an open book exam format. ICC’s journeyman exam outline lists the National Standard Journeyman Electrician exam as Open book—4 hour time limit. Open book is an advantage only when you prepare for it correctly. It doesn’t remove pressure; it shifts what the test is measuring. The exam rewards electricians who can find the right rule quickly and apply it accurately.

Open-book success comes down to a repeatable method:

  • Read the question twice before opening the book. Identify the real task: definition, requirement, exception, table value, or an application scenario.
  • Go to the code “neighborhood” first. Start at the likely chapter/article/part, then narrow down. Random flipping wastes time.
  • Confirm exceptions and notes every time. Many wrong answers happen when a candidate misses one exception or one table note.
  • Protect your pace. If a question becomes a time sink, move on and return later after you’ve secured easier points.

How this guide supports open-book testing:

  • Lookup-driven practice: questions designed to force you into the code and back out with the correct answer.
  • Navigation repetition: repeated exposure to the same NEC “neighborhoods” so lookups get faster naturally.
  • Exam-style wording: practice that trains careful reading and reduces “trap” mistakes.
  • Simulation pacing: full exams that train timing, stamina, and decision-making under pressure.

While each candidate’s documentation can differ, the general flow is consistent:

  1. Choose the correct Nevada electrical card type. Nevada uses journeyman and residential journeyman electrician exams (and other specialty exams) as part of the qualifications card program.
  2. Schedule the appropriate ICC exam. Nevada’s electrical exam information points candidates to the ICC Exam Catalog and notes testing options through Pearson VUE and ICC PRONTO (where available).

The biggest score gains usually come from tightening the same repeatable habits:

  • Stop losing points to exceptions: train yourself to look for exceptions and notes before committing to an answer.
  • Stop losing time to wandering: train the “neighborhood” method so you go directly to the right chapter/article/part.
  • Stop losing points to misreads: train yourself to slow down on wording that changes everything (“where required,” “shall not,” “maximum,” “minimum,” “nearest,” and “not less than”).
  • Stop losing points to table mistakes: train consistent table habits: read headings, confirm conditions, then read notes.

Here’s a practical way to use your 12 practice exams plus 2 full final exams like a complete prep system:

State Requirements

The Nevada C-17 classification authorizes a qualified license holder to perform the work included within the C-17 lathing and plastering subclassifications.

Lathing: This work includes selecting and applying wood and metal lath and other products designed to provide a base for plaster coatings. It can include channel iron used to support fireproof lath and solid plaster partitions within the authorized scope.

Plastering: This work includes coating surfaces with plaster made from materials such as sand, cement, quicklime, hydrated lime, and water, along with installation of lath or another suitable base for the plaster.

Drywall: The C-17 classification also includes the work authorized under the drywall subclassification, including installation and coating of gypsum wallboard and sheathing and installation of suspended ceiling systems made from gypsum wallboard.

Acoustical Tile: The classification includes installation of wood, mineral, fiber, and other types of acoustical tile by adhesives or other accepted methods, along with preparation of the installation surface.

Coatings of Stucco and Cement: The scope includes manual or mechanical application of stucco and cement coatings, preparation of surfaces, provision of the appropriate base for coatings, and related fireproofing work within the classification.

Studs of Sheet Metal: C-17 also includes erection and installation of sheet-metal studs used to frame ceilings and nonstructural partition walls.

For the standard Nevada licensing pathway, the Trade Qualified Individual must generally document at least four years of experience as a journeyman, foreman, supervising employee, or contractor in the specific classification requested. Financial responsibility, bonding, and background requirements are also part of Nevada contractor licensing. These requirements are separate from passing the trade examination and must be completed before the contractor license is issued.

Exam Details

The Nevada C-17F Studs of Sheet Metal Contractor examination is administered through PSI as part of the Nevada State Contractors Board licensing process. Nevada requires contractor applicants to submit their application and receive examination eligibility before scheduling the applicable trade examination.

The C-17F trade examination contains 20 questions. Candidates receive 1 hour to complete the examination and must answer 14 questions correctly to pass.

The examination content is divided into two primary areas:

  • Code Requirements: 4 questions.
  • Metal Framing Installation: 16 questions.

Metal Framing Installation represents 80 percent of the trade examination. Candidates should therefore spend most of their preparation time developing practical knowledge of nonstructural metal framing rather than relying entirely on code lookups.

Important preparation areas include wall layout, top and bottom tracks, vertical studs, stud spacing, framing around openings, ceiling framing, fasteners, attachment methods, alignment, connections, and coordination with surrounding construction.

The four Code Requirements questions require candidates to understand how the International Building Code applies to wall and ceiling assemblies, fire-resistance requirements, building materials, definitions, tables, exceptions, and related construction provisions.

Because the test contains only 20 questions, each question represents a significant percentage of the final score. Candidates should prepare carefully for both practical installation and code-navigation subjects.

Open Book Test

The Nevada C-17F Studs of Sheet Metal Contractor trade examination is an open-book test. The International Building Code, 2018 is the exam-room-approved trade reference included with this Ultimate package.

Nevada trade examinations are generally closed book except for specific code references identified for a particular classification. For C-17F, the International Building Code is the reference candidates may use during the trade examination.

Open-book testing does not eliminate the need for practical framing knowledge. Most of the C-17F examination is devoted to Metal Framing Installation, and candidates should be able to answer many installation questions based on their preparation and trade understanding.

The International Building Code should be used for targeted code lookups. Candidates should practice with the table of contents, index, definitions, tables, chapter organization, exceptions, and cross-references so the book can be used efficiently during the one-hour examination.

The supplied books are highlighted and tabbed for exam preparation. Using the prepared reference repeatedly before test day can help candidates become familiar with its organization rather than trying to learn the code layout during the examination.

The separate Nevada Business and Law examination, also known as the Construction Management Survey or CMS examination, is open book and permits use of the Construction Business and Law Manual for Nevada.

State Requirements

Nevada identifies C-17F as the Studs of Sheet Metal subclassification. The authorized scope covers the erection and installation of studs made of sheet metal for framing ceilings and nonstructural partitioning walls.

This classification is specifically focused on nonstructural sheet metal framing. Candidates should understand light-gauge metal framing systems and how those systems are installed as part of interior wall and ceiling construction.

Typical trade knowledge may include layout, tracks, studs, wall intersections, openings, ceiling framing, fasteners, attachment, alignment, and coordination with gypsum board and related building components.

The C-17F classification should not be confused with structural steel framing. The scope concerns studs of sheet metal used for ceilings and nonstructural partitioning walls rather than structural steel building frames.

Nevada contractor applicants must complete the applicable application and qualification requirements before the qualifying individual can receive authorization to test. The Nevada State Contractors Board states that an examination eligibility letter is issued after the application has been filed and the Board has verified applicable experience.

Nevada generally requires both the trade examination for the requested classification and the Business and Law, or CMS, examination unless the qualifying individual meets the requirements for an approved waiver.

Contractor licensing also involves requirements beyond examinations. Applicants must satisfy the other applicable Nevada State Contractors Board requirements associated with the business and contractor license before the license is issued.

Test Information and Study Materials

A productive Nevada C-17F study plan should give most of its attention to Metal Framing Installation because that subject represents 16 of the 20 examination questions.

Begin with the primary components used in nonstructural sheet metal framing. Candidates should understand how studs and tracks work together, how walls are laid out, and how the framing system is positioned before installation begins.

Stud installation should include spacing, orientation, alignment, placement within tracks, fastening, and coordination with openings and adjacent construction. Candidates should understand how consistent installation affects the completed wall assembly.

Track installation should include layout, positioning, attachment, alignment, and the relationship between tracks and vertical framing members. Proper track placement establishes the boundaries of the wall and influences the alignment of the studs.

Openings deserve dedicated preparation. Doors, access panels, and other wall interruptions may require additional framing or altered stud placement. Candidates should understand the practical principles used to frame these conditions.

Ceiling framing is specifically included within the C-17F classification. Review the relationship between metal framing members, support conditions, alignment, attachment, and coordination with surrounding wall and ceiling systems.

Fasteners and connections should also be studied. Candidates should understand why proper attachment matters and how fastening methods contribute to alignment and stability within a nonstructural framing assembly.

Measurement and layout are essential trade concepts. Improper layout can affect wall location, openings, ceiling framing, and the installation of finish materials that follow the framing work.

The four Code Requirements questions make International Building Code navigation an important secondary part of preparation. Practice finding information involving wall assemblies, ceilings, fire resistance, construction materials, definitions, and related provisions.

The IBC index is useful when the exact section is unknown. Identify the principal term in the question and use the index to narrow the search. Once the section is found, read enough surrounding text to understand whether an exception, table, note, or cross-reference affects the requirement.

Definitions should also receive attention because building-code terminology can have a specific meaning. A candidate who understands the defined term can often identify the correct code path more quickly.

Timed practice is especially useful for a 20-question examination. Candidates have approximately three minutes per question on average, but practical framing questions may be answered more quickly, leaving additional time for targeted code lookups.

Use mixed practice after individual subjects become familiar. Alternating between installation questions and code-based questions can help candidates become accustomed to changing topics during the actual exam.

The Nevada Business and Law examination should receive separate study time. Use the Construction Business and Law Manual for Nevada during preparation so its organization becomes familiar before taking the open-book CMS examination.

The C-15A examination covers major roofing knowledge areas, including safety, roofing substrates, steep roofing, repairs, elastomeric roofing, built-up bituminous roofing, sheet metal and flashing, and photovoltaic-related roofing considerations.

Steep Roofing represents the largest individual area of the examination. Candidates should spend significant preparation time on asphalt shingles, clay and concrete tile, wood shakes and shingles, slate, roof decks, underlayments, fastening, flashing, valleys, ridges, penetrations, drainage, and installation practices associated with steep-slope systems.

Built-up Bituminous Roofing and Elastomeric Roofing require knowledge of low-slope roofing systems, membranes, insulation, flashing, attachment, surfacing, repairs, and installation practices. The NRCA roofing manuals are valuable study resources for these subjects.

Sheet Metal and Flashing may represent a smaller portion of the examination, but flashing is fundamental to watertight roof construction. Candidates should understand the role of flashings at walls, penetrations, valleys, edges, roof transitions, and other vulnerable locations.

Licensing Steps

  1. Select the Nevada B-2 classification. The Residential and Small Commercial classification is intended for qualifying construction and remodeling work on structures that do not exceed three stories above ground and one story below ground.
  2. Identify the qualifying individual or individuals. Nevada requires each contractor license to have a qualified individual. One individual may serve in both management and trade qualifying roles, or separate individuals may fulfill those responsibilities.
  3. Document the required trade experience. The trade qualified individual generally must demonstrate at least four full years of applicable experience as a journeyman, foreman, supervising employee, or contractor within the 15 years immediately preceding the application.
  4. Submit the Nevada contractor license application. The application is submitted to the Nevada State Contractors Board with the required business, qualifier, financial, background, and experience information.
  5. Receive examination eligibility. Candidates may not schedule the Nevada contractor examinations until the application has been submitted, experience has been reviewed, and the Board issues authorization.
  6. Pass the required examinations. A management qualifier must pass the Nevada Construction Management Survey examination. The trade qualifier must satisfy the B-2 trade examination requirement unless an applicable waiver is granted.
  7. Complete remaining licensing requirements. Applicants must satisfy the Board's financial responsibility and licensing requirements before the contractor license is issued.
  8. Provide the required contractor bond after approval. Nevada requires contractor licenses to be supported by a license bond, with the required amount determined by the Board.

The management qualified individual is responsible for satisfying the business and law examination requirement. Nevada recognizes C-15 Roofing and Siding as a specialty contractor classification. The classification encompasses roofing and siding work and includes the work authorized under its applicable subclassifications.

The roofing portion includes installation, application, alteration, and repair of watertight and weatherproof materials used on roofs. Roofing systems can include a variety of coverings and materials used to protect buildings from weather.

The siding portion covers installation, alteration, and repair of siding used to make exterior walls watertight and weatherproof. Candidates should understand how siding integrates with sheathing, openings, soffits, flashing, trim, and other exterior wall components.

The broader C-15 classification also encompasses related insulation and waterproofing work authorized under its subclassifications. Masonry work requires an understanding of much more than placing individual units. Contractors must understand layout, mortar, grout, reinforcement, anchors, walls, openings, structural support, building-code requirements, and proper installation methods.

The International Building Code supports the broader building-code side of the classification, while ACI 530/530.1 addresses more specialized structural masonry requirements. Candidates should understand how both references work together when preparing for the trade examination.

Practical masonry knowledge is also important. Brick, block, stone, mortar, reinforcement, tools, layout, joint work, wall construction, and material handling are all parts of the trade that can affect workmanship and system performance.

Safety should remain part of the overall preparation process because masonry can involve elevated work, cutting, lifting, scaffolds, ladders, heavy materials, and other jobsite hazards.
