A strong Nevada C-18 preparation plan should combine practical masonry knowledge, structural masonry requirements, building-code navigation, jobsite safety, business and law study, and practice-oriented course preparation.

Brick and Block Construction should include unit selection, layout, coursing, bonding, alignment, joint work, openings, and complete wall construction. Candidates should understand how individual masonry units contribute to the finished assembly.

Mortar and Grout should be reviewed as separate materials serving different purposes. Candidates should understand the role of mortar between masonry units and the role of grout in reinforced or filled masonry construction.

Reinforcement should receive focused study. Candidates should understand reinforcing steel, placement, interaction with grout, wall systems, openings, and the way reinforcement contributes to structural performance.

Stone Masonry should include material selection, placement, cutting, bonding, support, and finishing. Stone work differs from standard brick and block construction and should be studied as a distinct masonry area.

Wall Layout and Construction should include dimensions, corners, lines, levels, plumb conditions, coursing, and proper sequencing. Accurate layout is essential because small deviations can affect the completed wall.

Openings and Supports should include lintels, bearing, reinforcement, anchors, and the way doors, windows, and other penetrations affect a masonry wall.

Flashing and Moisture Control should also receive attention. Candidates should understand how moisture can affect masonry construction and why proper detailing contributes to durability.

Scaffolds and Ladders should receive dedicated OSHA review because masonry work often occurs above ground level. Candidates should understand safe access, working platforms, fall hazards, and proper equipment use.

Exam Details

The Nevada C-15 Roofing and Siding Contractor examination is administered through PSI as part of the Nevada State Contractors Board licensing process. A contractor applicant must first submit the required license application and receive examination eligibility before scheduling the trade examination.

The C-15 trade examination contains 60 questions. Candidates must answer at least 45 questions correctly to achieve the published minimum passing score. The examination allows 2 hours for completion.

The published Nevada C-15 examination content outline includes:

  • Safety: 5 questions.
  • Roofing Substrates: 8 questions.
  • Steep Roofing: 16 questions.
  • Roofing Repairs: 4 questions.
  • Elastomeric Roofing: 7 questions.
  • Built-up Bituminous Roofing: 7 questions.
  • Sheet Metal and Flashing: 3 questions.
  • Siding: 8 questions.
  • Photovoltaic Systems: 2 questions.

Steep roofing represents the largest individual portion of the examination, accounting for 16 of the 60 questions. Roofing substrates and siding each represent eight questions, while elastomeric roofing and built-up bituminous roofing each represent seven. Safety, roofing repairs, sheet metal and flashing, and photovoltaic systems make up the remainder of the published outline.

Candidates should prepare across the complete outline. A strong study strategy gives additional attention to the larger categories while still reviewing the smaller sections because questions can come from every published subject area.

Open Book Test

The Nevada C-15 Roofing and Siding Contractor examination is an open-book test. The International Building Code, 2018 is identified as an approved reference for the C-15 examination room.

PSI requires candidates to bring their own approved reference material to the testing center. Reference materials may be highlighted, underlined, and indexed before the examination. Written notes are not permitted in the references, and candidates may not write in or add highlighting to the books during the examination session.

Permanent tabs may be used to organize approved examination references. Temporary or removable tabs are not permitted. Loose or attached additional papers are also prohibited under PSI reference-material rules.

Open-book testing does not eliminate the need to learn the trade. The C-15 examination is based on roofing and siding knowledge, general industry practices, and technical references. Candidates should understand common systems, materials, installation methods, repair practices, safety considerations, and code concepts before test day.

Reference navigation should be practiced along with technical review. When working with the International Building Code, become familiar with the index, chapter structure, definitions, tables, roof assembly provisions, exterior wall requirements, materials, and other sections connected to roofing and siding work.

Licensing Steps

The Nevada State Contractors Board licenses businesses and individuals that perform contracting work within the state. Candidates pursuing the C-15 classification must satisfy the licensing requirements applicable to the business and the qualifying individual.

  1. Select the C-15 Roofing and Siding classification. Applicants seeking authority to perform work within the complete Nevada roofing and siding specialty apply for the C-15 classification.
  2. Identify the qualifying individual. Nevada requires the applicant to identify a person who has the necessary experience, knowledge, and skills to qualify the business in the requested classification.
  3. Document qualifying trade experience. The trade qualified individual must generally demonstrate at least four full years of applicable experience as a journeyman, foreman, supervising employee, or contractor in the requested classification within the 15 years immediately before the application is filed.
  4. Submit the contractor license application. The applicant submits the required business, qualifying individual, experience, financial, and supporting information to the Nevada State Contractors Board.
  5. Receive examination eligibility. The trade examination cannot be scheduled until the application has been submitted and the Board has issued examination eligibility.
  6. Complete the C-15 trade examination. The trade qualifying individual must satisfy the Roofing and Siding examination requirement unless an applicable waiver has been approved.
  7. Complete the Business and Law requirement. Nevada generally requires the appropriate qualifying individual to pass the Construction Management Survey business and law examination unless a qualifying waiver applies.
  8. Complete remaining licensing requirements. The applicant must satisfy the Nevada State Contractors Board's applicable financial responsibility, background, bonding, and other licensing requirements before the license can be issued.

State Requirements

The Nevada C-15 classification is the Roofing and Siding specialty classification. A contractor holding the full C-15 classification may perform work authorized within the associated roofing and siding subclassifications and related areas included in the classification scope.

The roofing portion of the classification includes installation, application, alteration, and repair of watertight and weatherproof roofing materials. Nevada regulations identify materials such as asphalt, pitch, tar, felt, shakes, shingles, aluminum, tile, slate, urethane, and qualifying photovoltaic roof tiles.

The siding portion includes installation, alteration, and repair of siding materials used to make the walls of a structure watertight and weatherproof. Materials can include wood, aluminum, enameled steel, plastic, and glass. The broader C-15 scope also includes insulation and waterproofing work within the limits established by Nevada regulations.

The trade qualified individual generally must have four years of qualifying experience in the requested classification within the 15 years immediately preceding the application. Qualifying experience may be obtained as a journeyman, foreman, supervising employee, or contractor.

Nevada does not require a specific college degree to obtain a contractor license. Accepted education or training may be used toward a portion of the experience requirement when it meets Nevada State Contractors Board standards and is properly documented.

The Nevada State Contractors Board also requires applicants to demonstrate financial responsibility. Contractor licensing can include financial statement requirements, bank verification, bonding, and other application documentation in addition to examination qualification.

Reference Books

  • International Building Code, 2018
    A building code reference covering roof assemblies, exterior walls, materials, fire-resistance requirements, structural concepts, weather protection, and other building provisions. This edition is also identified as an approved reference for the Nevada C-15 examination room.
  • NRCA Roofing Manual: Steep Slope Roof Systems, 2025
    A roofing industry reference focused on steep-slope roof systems. It supports review of materials, system components, installation principles, flashing, roof coverings, and other steep-roofing subjects that receive substantial emphasis on the C-15 examination.
  • NRCA Roofing Manual: Metal Panel and SPF Roof Systems, 2024
    A technical roofing reference covering metal panel roofing and spray polyurethane foam roofing systems, including materials, assemblies, components, installation principles, and industry practices.
  • NRCA Roofing Manual: Membrane Roofing Systems
    A technical reference addressing membrane roof systems and low-slope roofing concepts. It supports study of elastomeric and other membrane-related roofing subjects found within C-15 preparation.

    The federal construction safety regulations used to study workplace hazards, worker protection, fall protection, ladders, scaffolds, personal protective equipment, and other safety subjects relevant to roofing and siding operations.
  • Standard Practice for Installation of Rigid Poly(Vinyl Chloride) (PVC) Siding and Soffit - ASTM D 4756
    An industry standard addressing installation practices for rigid PVC siding and soffit. It supports preparation for the siding portion of the C-15 examination.

    A roofing reference covering roofing materials, construction methods, estimating concepts, measurements, and practical trade information useful for reviewing roofing systems and project calculations.
  • Carpentry and Building Construction, 2016
    A general construction reference covering building materials, structural components, carpentry concepts, framing, and related construction practices that can support understanding of roof substrates and building assemblies.
  • NRCA Guidelines for Roof Systems with Rooftop Photovoltaic Components, 2018
    A roofing industry reference focused on the relationship between roof systems and rooftop photovoltaic components. It supports preparation for the photovoltaic portion of the Nevada C-15 examination.

The examination also includes photovoltaic systems. Candidates should review how rooftop photovoltaic components interact with roof assemblies, including penetrations, flashing, water management, roof access, system placement, and protection of the underlying roofing system.

Timed practice is also valuable. With 60 questions in two hours, candidates should avoid spending too much time searching for a single answer. Developing a disciplined process for answering, marking difficult questions, and returning to them can improve time management during preparation.

Special Applications and Accessories includes work beyond basic wallboard installation. Candidates should review suspended gypsum wallboard ceilings, specialty conditions, trims, accessories, and other applications that may require different installation or finishing methods.

Taping and finishing should also receive substantial attention. Review joint treatment, tape, joint compounds, corner treatments, finishing sequences, surface preparation, and techniques used to produce finished gypsum wallboard surfaces.

Gypsum materials and systems are another important part of preparation. Candidates should be familiar with different gypsum panel products, sheathing, fasteners, compounds, accessories, trims, and assemblies and understand how they are used in different construction conditions.

Acoustical tile is included within the C-3E scope and should not be overlooked. Candidates should review the basic materials, components, and installation considerations associated with acoustical ceiling work.

Sheet-metal studs for ceilings and nonstructural partitioning are also included in the C-3E scope. Candidates should understand how these framing systems relate to drywall installation, layout, attachment, and finished partition systems.

The C-38A Pipes and Vents subclassification includes installation of pipes from the source of liquefied petroleum or natural gas supply into a building or other structure and installation of related vents. Its scope also includes installation of and connections to above-ground tanks containing liquefied petroleum or natural gas.

The C-38B Gas Appliances and Equipment subclassification includes installation of appliances and equipment requiring connection to a supply of liquefied petroleum or natural gas.

The C-38C Heating and Ventilating subclassification includes fabrication and installation of systems used to heat air with liquefied petroleum or natural gas and circulate that air.

The full C-38 classification therefore involves several connected areas of trade knowledge. Candidates should understand the gas supply, piping, appliances, equipment, venting, combustion, and heating-system requirements that work together in a complete installation.

  • Piping: 15 questions
  • Water Cooling Equipment: 10 questions

  • Safety: 7 questions

Piping is the largest individual section of the C-21F examination. Candidates should review piping materials, fittings, joining methods, supports, layouts, equipment connections, circulation, flow relationships, valves, and applicable mechanical and plumbing-code requirements.

Water Cooling Equipment accounts for 10 questions. Candidates should understand chillers, cooling towers, coils, pumps, system circulation, heat transfer, storage components, and the basic operating relationships found in chilled-water systems.

Water Heating Equipment also accounts for 10 questions. Preparation should include boilers, pumps, tanks, piping, controls, valves, and the equipment used to generate, circulate, and transfer heated water.

Valves and Controls represents eight questions. Candidates should understand the function of common valves, control devices, temperature-control components, flow-control devices, and related equipment used to regulate hydronic systems.

Safety represents seven questions. Candidates should prepare for jobsite hazards, personal protective equipment, tools, ladders, material handling, fall protection, and other construction-safety requirements applicable to mechanical-system installation.

State Requirements

Nevada recognizes C-21D Maintenance as a subclassification under C-21 Refrigeration and Air-Conditioning.

The classification covers the repair and replacement of parts of existing air-conditioning and refrigeration units or systems. This can include compressors, motors, relays, coils, heat exchangers, and related equipment used to keep existing systems operating properly.

The scope is maintenance-oriented rather than design-oriented. C-21D work focuses on servicing existing systems and replacing components while remaining within the original system design.

The classification does not include work that alters the design of an existing system. It also does not include certain major equipment replacements, including complete condenser assemblies on remote systems and air handlers.

This distinction is important for exam preparation because the C-21D classification emphasizes service, diagnostics, maintenance, repair, component replacement, and system testing rather than complete HVAC installation or redesign.

A productive Nevada C-21D preparation plan should combine strong troubleshooting knowledge with regular use of the Uniform Mechanical Code.

The Refrigeration Cycle should be one of the first technical subjects reviewed. Candidates should understand compression, condensation, expansion, and evaporation and how refrigerant pressure and temperature change through each stage.

Compressors are central to refrigeration and air-conditioning systems. Candidates should understand compressor function, pressure relationships, lubrication, electrical operation, overheating, abnormal operating conditions, and common failure symptoms.

Condensers should be studied in relation to heat rejection, airflow, coil cleanliness, fan operation, ambient temperature, and system pressure. Restricted airflow or dirty coils can significantly affect system performance.

Evaporators should be reviewed in relation to heat absorption, airflow, refrigerant condition, icing, condensate management, and overall system capacity.

Metering Devices should be studied according to their role in controlling refrigerant flow and creating the pressure difference needed for the refrigeration cycle. Candidates should understand how improper operation can affect evaporator performance and system pressures.

Refrigerant System Troubleshooting should include recognition of abnormal suction and discharge pressures, airflow restrictions, refrigerant restrictions, improper charge, component problems, and other conditions that can reduce system performance.

Controls and Electrical Components should include thermostats, relays, contactors, capacitors, transformers, pressure switches, solenoid valves, motors, and safety controls.

Maintenance technicians should understand how to distinguish between an electrical-control problem and a refrigeration-system problem. A compressor that does not start, for example, can result from several different electrical, control, or mechanical causes.

Motors and Blowers should be reviewed in relation to airflow, electrical operation, bearings, capacitors, rotation, speed, and mechanical condition. Poor airflow can affect comfort, equipment performance, coil temperatures, and refrigeration pressures.

Coils and Heat Exchangers should be studied in relation to heat transfer, airflow, cleanliness, operating condition, and maintenance. Dirty or damaged heat-transfer surfaces can affect both efficiency and system performance.

Piping and Tubing should include line function, materials, fittings, supports, insulation, leaks, restrictions, routing, and service practices. Candidates should understand how piping conditions can influence refrigerant flow, oil return, and pressure drop.

Testing and Diagnosis should include evaluation of pressure, temperature, airflow, electrical measurements, component operation, and overall system behavior. Troubleshooting should follow a systematic process rather than guessing which component needs replacement.

Preventive Maintenance is also important. Candidates should understand routine inspection of filters, coils, motors, electrical connections, condensate systems, refrigerant lines, controls, and other components that can affect system reliability.

Because the exam contains 60 questions in two hours, pacing should be practiced. Candidates should avoid spending too much time on one difficult code search. If necessary, move on and return to the question later.

A service-oriented study sequence can help organize preparation. Start with the refrigeration cycle, then move through compressors, condensers, evaporators, metering devices, controls, motors, airflow, piping, testing, and troubleshooting.

A strong Nevada C-21A preparation plan should combine refrigeration knowledge with repeated navigation of the Uniform Mechanical Code.

Refrigeration and Refrigerants should receive the largest share of study time because it represents 17 of the 50 exam questions. Candidates should understand the refrigeration cycle and how the compressor, condenser, expansion device, and evaporator work together.

Study refrigerant pressure and temperature relationships, heat absorption, heat rejection, system conditions, and the role of each major component. Understanding the system as a complete cycle can make technical questions easier to analyze.

Compressors should be reviewed in relation to refrigerant flow, pressure changes, lubrication, operating conditions, and system performance. Candidates should understand the purpose of the compressor within the refrigeration cycle and recognize common system relationships.

Condensers should be studied as heat-rejection devices. Candidates should understand the difference between common condenser arrangements and how airflow or water flow affects system performance.

Cooling Towers should be reviewed in connection with heat rejection, water circulation, maintenance, and mechanical-system operation.

Evaporators should be studied in relation to heat absorption, airflow, refrigerant boiling, temperature control, and the overall cooling process.

Piping and Tubing deserves significant attention because it accounts for 8 questions. Review piping materials, fittings, brazed or joined connections, supports, insulation, routing, pressure drop, and oil return.

Candidates should understand the basic differences among suction lines, liquid lines, and discharge lines and how improper piping can affect refrigeration-system operation.

Controls, Valves and Wiring should include thermostats, relays, contactors, pressure switches, solenoid valves, expansion devices, safety controls, and basic control circuits.

Refrigeration controls are used to regulate temperature, manage refrigerant flow, start and stop equipment, and protect the system from unsafe operating conditions. Candidates should understand the purpose of each control rather than memorizing terminology alone.

Walk-ins and Box Construction should include insulated panels, doors, vapor protection, temperature maintenance, equipment coordination, and the relationship between the enclosure and refrigeration system.

Ducts and Ventilation should include airflow, blowers, registers, ductwork, ventilation requirements, and how air movement relates to refrigeration equipment and conditioned spaces.

Testing and Inspection should include system checks, leak detection concepts, pressure testing, equipment inspection, and recognition of installation or operating conditions that may require correction.

Gas preparation should include the gas-related work permitted within the C-21A scope and the connection between refrigeration equipment and fuel supply.

Safety should also be studied as part of the complete trade. Refrigeration contractors may work around electrical equipment, pressurized systems, ladders, tools, piping, refrigerants, moving equipment, and mechanical rooms.

Candidates should also practice pacing. If a code search is taking too long, it may be better to move forward and return later rather than spend several minutes on one question.

Licensing Steps

  1. Confirm the C-20 classification. Make sure the Nevada Tiling classification matches the type of contracting work the business intends to perform.
  2. Identify the qualifying individual. The Nevada contractor application must identify the person responsible for satisfying the applicable qualification requirements.
  3. Prepare qualifying experience information. Organize the applicable work-history documentation related to tile installation and the requested classification.
  4. Submit the Nevada contractor license application. Complete the applicable application and supporting documentation.
  5. Receive examination eligibility. After applicable application and qualification requirements are addressed, proceed with required testing.
  6. Prepare for the C-20 trade examination. Study Surface Preparation, Installation and Adhesives, and Grout and Finishing.
  7. Use the study references actively. Work through practical installation concepts, industry standards, floor systems, and tile-setting methods.
  8. Prepare for applicable Nevada contractor business requirements. Complete the required business and law preparation associated with contractor licensing.
  9. Complete the required examinations. Take the applicable trade and contractor business examinations.
  10. Complete remaining licensing requirements. Finish the other applicable requirements associated with contractor license issuance.

State Requirements

Nevada designates C-20 as the specialty classification for Tiling.

A Nevada C-20 contractor may install, by means of suction and adhesives, ceramic tile, encaustic tile, vitreous tile, and other tile-like products, except for hollow or structural partitioning tile.

The C-20 classification therefore focuses on surface preparation and tile installation rather than structural partition tile work. Candidates should understand how tile products are installed over suitable surfaces and how substrate conditions, bonding materials, and finishing procedures affect the completed installation.

The C-20 classification also includes designated subclassifications covering plastic tile and wallboard and swimming pool tile and coping. Candidates seeking the full C-20 classification should prepare for the scope applicable to the broader tiling specialty.

Tile contractors must understand the relationship among the substrate, setting material, tile product, grout, movement considerations, and finished surface. A problem with one part of that system can affect the entire installation.

The C-20 trade examination is one part of Nevada contractor licensing. Applicants must also satisfy applicable qualification, application, business, financial, and administrative requirements before a contractor license is issued.

Reference Books

    This used study reference supports preparation involving tile layout, cutting, setting techniques, substrate conditions, mortars, adhesives, joints, grouting, finishing, and practical field procedures used in tile installation.

  • ANSI A108/A118/A136.1:2017, American National Standard Specifications for the Installation of Ceramic Tile, 2017
    This technical study reference supports preparation involving recognized ceramic tile installation procedures, setting-material specifications, mortars, adhesives, material performance, and standardized installation practices.

Test Information and Study Materials

A strong Nevada C-20 study plan should begin with Surface Preparation. Tile installations depend on the quality and suitability of the surface receiving the tile, so candidates should understand how to inspect, prepare, clean, level, and evaluate substrates before setting work begins.

Study common floor and wall conditions that can affect tile installation. Candidates should understand why flatness, cleanliness, stability, and surface condition matter to proper bonding.

The Builders Guide to Floors, 1997 can help reinforce knowledge of floor construction, subfloor systems, underlayments, leveling, and support conditions. Understanding the floor beneath the tile can help candidates recognize installation problems before tile is placed.

Moisture should be considered during surface preparation because inappropriate moisture conditions can affect setting materials, substrates, and completed installations.

Surface cleaning is another basic but important topic. Dust, debris, coatings, contaminants, and other conditions can interfere with bonding between the tile-setting material and the substrate.

Installation and Adhesives deserves the greatest study emphasis because it represents 22 questions, more than half of the examination.

Candidates should understand the differences among common setting methods and the role of mortars, adhesives, and related bonding products. Focus on matching the setting material to the tile, substrate, and installation environment.

Setting Tile, 1995 (USED) can help candidates study practical tile installation techniques, including layout, cutting, fitting, mortar application, adhesive use, setting, and finishing.

Layout is a core tiling skill. Candidates should understand how tile placement affects appearance, cuts, joints, transitions, and the overall balance of the finished installation.

Practice working through layout decisions mentally. Consider how a room, wall, opening, corner, or obstruction can affect starting points and cut-tile placement.

Cutting and fitting should also receive attention. Tile frequently must be fitted around edges, corners, penetrations, fixtures, and other building components.

Mortar application is important because proper contact between the tile, setting material, and substrate contributes to a reliable installation. Candidates should understand appropriate application practices and why consistent coverage matters.

Adhesive selection should be studied in relation to the tile product, substrate, and installation condition. Different materials and environments may require different setting products.

The ANSI A108/A118/A136.1:2017 reference can help candidates understand recognized standards governing installation methods and setting materials. Use it to connect practical field techniques with formal industry requirements.

Rather than trying to memorize every standard number, focus on the practical purpose of the requirements. Understand why certain materials, preparation methods, or installation practices are used and what problem each requirement is designed to prevent.

Tile spacing and joints should also be studied. Candidates should understand how consistent joints contribute to appearance and how joint planning relates to tile dimensions and the finished surface.

Movement within the substrate or tile assembly can affect installations. Candidates should understand why tile systems must accommodate expected building and material movement.

Grout and Finishing represents 6 questions and should not be neglected. Review grout preparation, placement, joint filling, cleanup, final surface treatment, and finishing procedures.

Candidates should understand why the grout must be properly worked into the joints and why timing can affect cleanup and the finished appearance.

Grout joints should be studied as part of the complete installation rather than as a final cosmetic step. Joint condition, depth, cleanliness, and material selection can affect performance.

Finishing should include attention to the completed surface, joint appearance, cleanup, transitions, edges, and other details that affect professional workmanship.

Because the examination is closed book, candidates should convert the information in the references into retained knowledge. Active recall is particularly useful for procedures that follow a sequence.

For example, study a floor tile installation and then explain the entire process from memory: inspect the substrate, prepare the surface, establish the layout, select the setting material, spread the mortar or adhesive, place and align the tile, allow the installation to develop appropriately, grout the joints, and complete the finishing work.

Another useful exercise is to compare installation conditions. Ask how the approach might change based on the substrate, tile type, setting material, or location.

Create separate study sessions for Surface Preparation, Installation and Adhesives, and Grout and Finishing. Because the exam weighting is not equal, allocate the most time to Installation and Adhesives.

A practical study schedule might spend more than half of trade-preparation time on installation and bonding concepts, followed by concentrated surface-preparation review and regular grout and finishing practice.

Once individual topics are familiar, move into mixed practice. The actual examination may move from a substrate question to an adhesive question and then to grout or finishing without warning.

When a practice question is missed, determine whether the issue came from unfamiliar terminology, weak knowledge of setting materials, confusion about substrate preparation, or misunderstanding of installation standards.

Return to the relevant reference and study the concept rather than memorizing only the correct answer. Closed-book examinations reward candidates who understand why an installation method is appropriate.

Timed practice is also useful. With 40 questions in 1.5 hours, candidates should learn to answer familiar trade questions efficiently and avoid spending too much time on a single difficult item.

As the examination approaches, focus on active recall, mixed-topic practice, terminology review, and installation sequences. The goal is to recognize common trade situations and apply the appropriate tile-setting principles without depending on the books during the test.

State Requirements

Nevada recognizes C-14A Reinforcing Steel as a subclassification under C-14 Steel Reinforcing and Erection.

The authorized scope includes the fabrication, placement, and tying of steel reinforcing bars or rods, and post-tensioning used to reinforce concrete buildings and structures.

This means the classification covers both conventional reinforcing steel and post-tensioning activities within reinforced concrete construction. Candidates should understand reinforcing bars as part of a complete structural system rather than as isolated pieces of steel.

Reinforcing work begins before concrete is placed. Contractors may need to interpret reinforcing drawings, identify bars, coordinate deliveries, stage material, fabricate or prepare reinforcing assemblies, place supports, install bars, tie intersections, maintain spacing, and coordinate with formwork and embedded items.

During concrete placement, reinforcement must remain in the intended position. Field crews need to understand how movement, inadequate supports, improper tying, interference with other trades, or careless concrete operations can affect the finished work.

Post-tensioning adds another level of specialized knowledge. Tendons and anchorages must be installed and handled according to the intended system, and stressing operations require careful procedures and strict attention to safety.

The C-14A trade examination is one part of the Nevada contractor licensing process. Applicants must also satisfy applicable qualification, application, Business and Law, and other licensing requirements before a contractor license is issued.

Reference Books

Because the C-14A examination is closed book, candidates should develop strong recall of relevant safety concepts.
  • Placing Reinforcing Bars

Test Information and Study Materials

A strong Nevada C-14A study plan should begin with reinforcing-bar fundamentals. Candidates should understand common reinforcing terminology, bar identification, placement concepts, supports, ties, splices, clearances, bends, and how reinforcing steel is shown on drawings.

Bar Placement should receive significant attention. Reinforcement must be installed in the intended location and maintained there while concrete is placed. Candidates should understand the purpose of chairs, bolsters, spacers, ties, and other supports used to maintain position.

Tying Reinforcement should be studied as a field procedure. Different reinforcing configurations may require different tying approaches, and ties help keep bars properly positioned during construction. Candidates should understand the practical purpose of tying rather than viewing it as a purely mechanical task.

Splices and Development should be reviewed as part of reinforcing continuity. Candidates should understand basic lap-splice concepts, mechanical connection concepts, bar continuity, and why reinforcing details must match the structural design.

Bar Identification and Detailing should include the information used to distinguish bar sizes, shapes, locations, quantities, and fabrication requirements. The CRSI Manual of Standard Practice can help candidates become more familiar with industry conventions.

Reinforcing Drawings should be studied carefully. Candidates should practice reading plans and details showing slabs, beams, walls, columns, footings, reinforcing mats, openings, additional reinforcement, and other structural conditions.

Plan-reading practice is particularly valuable for a closed-book examination because candidates need to recognize reinforcing relationships without relying on a reference during the test.

Concrete Cover should be understood as part of reinforcing placement. The location of reinforcing steel within a concrete member affects protection, durability, and structural behavior. Candidates should understand why bars cannot simply be positioned wherever installation is easiest.

Field Coordination is another important topic. Reinforcement frequently intersects with formwork, sleeves, conduits, embedded items, anchor bolts, openings, and other trades. Candidates should understand the need to follow the design while coordinating conflicts appropriately.

Material Handling should be reviewed because reinforcing bars are heavy, long, and difficult to move safely. Bundled reinforcing steel may require cranes or other equipment, and improper handling can expose workers to crushing, struck-by, pinch-point, and lifting hazards.

Post-Tensioning should receive dedicated study time because it is specifically included in the C-14A scope. Candidates should understand the basic purpose of post-tensioning and how tendons are used to apply compressive forces to concrete.

Study the basic components of an unbonded post-tensioning system, including the tendon, prestressing steel, protective sheathing, anchorages, wedges, stressing equipment, and related hardware.

Tendon Installation should include placement, support, routing, coordination, protection, and preparation for concrete placement. Tendons must be maintained in the intended profile and protected from damage before stressing.

Stressing Operations require particular attention to procedure and safety. Candidates should understand the purpose of stressing, the role of anchors and wedges, and why personnel must remain clear of hazardous areas during stressing operations.

Post-Tensioning Safety should be treated as a major study subject. High forces are involved, and improper procedures can create serious hazards. Candidates should understand controlled work areas, equipment condition, worker positioning, communication, and safe handling practices.

OSHA Construction Safety should be integrated throughout the study process. Reinforcing-steel work can involve elevated surfaces, floor openings, protruding reinforcing bars, material handling, cranes, tools, formwork, concrete placement, and fall exposure.

Fall Protection deserves attention because reinforcing-steel installers often work on elevated walls, decks, columns, and structural members. Candidates should understand basic fall-hazard recognition and the importance of suitable protection and access.

Impalement Hazards should also be reviewed. Protruding reinforcing steel can create severe hazards when workers are exposed to falls or movement around unfinished reinforcing assemblies.

Personal Protective Equipment should be understood in relation to the task being performed. Reinforcing work may require appropriate head, eye, hand, foot, and fall protection depending on field conditions.

Because the examination is closed book, candidates should gradually shift away from reading and toward active recall. Study a topic, close the reference, and explain the key steps, terminology, or safety requirements from memory.

Flashcards can help with bar terminology, post-tensioning components, safety concepts, and common field practices. Practice questions can help determine whether the information is being retained well enough to use without a reference.

A useful study sequence is to move from reinforcing fundamentals to bar placement, drawings, supports, ties, splices, post-tensioning, field safety, and then mixed practice. This allows candidates to build a foundation before combining subjects in exam-style review.

Active recall is especially important for this examination. Repeatedly answering questions without the books nearby can help candidates become more comfortable applying trade knowledge in a closed-book setting.

State Requirements

Nevada's B-2 Residential and Small Commercial classification covers construction and remodeling of houses and other structures that support, shelter, or enclose persons, animals, or property and that do not extend more than three stories above ground and one story below ground.

The B-2 classification is a general building classification within those size limits. Candidates should understand the full construction process rather than concentrating on only one specialty trade.

A B-2 contractor may coordinate multiple phases of work, including site preparation, foundations, structural framing, masonry, roofing, weather protection, doors, windows, drywall, finishes, and other construction activities needed to complete a building.

General building authority does not automatically mean every specialty trade can be self-performed. Electrical, plumbing, HVAC, fire protection, and other specialty work require the applicable authority when performed directly.

The Nevada B-2 examination is one part of the licensing process. Applicants must also satisfy applicable qualification, application, business and law, financial, and other contractor licensing requirements before a license is issued.

Test Information and Study Materials

A productive Nevada B-2 study plan should follow the sequence of a building project. Begin with sitework and foundations, then move through concrete, masonry, framing, enclosure, openings, interior finishes, safety, plan reading, and estimating.

Sitework preparation should include grading, excavation, drainage, trenches, soil conditions, compaction, and preparation for foundation work. Candidates should understand how poor site preparation can affect the building above it.

Concrete should include footings, foundations, slabs, reinforcement, formwork, placement, consolidation, finishing, curing, and structural requirements. Use ACI 318 for reinforced structural concrete provisions and the Contractor's Guide for practical field study.

Masonry preparation should include brick, block, stone, mortar, walls, layout, reinforcement concepts, and coordination with other building systems.

Carpentry should include floors, walls, roofs, sheathing, openings, headers, stairs, fastening, framing layout, and construction sequencing. Residential framing questions may often lead candidates to the IRC.

Wood Trusses should be studied for handling, installation, restraint, and bracing. The BCSI guide is included for study so candidates can strengthen understanding of truss-related field practices.

Thermal and Moisture Protection should include roofing, flashing, weather barriers, waterproofing, insulation, drainage, and methods used to protect the building enclosure from moisture.

Doors and Windows should be reviewed in relation to openings, structural coordination, installation, flashing, weather protection, and applicable code requirements.

Drywall and Finishes should include gypsum materials, wall and ceiling systems, framing coordination, fastening, finishing, and common installation practices.

Safety should be studied independently because OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926 is not allowed into the exam room. Candidates should develop retained knowledge involving fall protection, ladders, scaffolds, excavation hazards, electrical safety, tools, material handling, and personal protective equipment.

Plan Reading should include floor plans, foundation plans, elevations, sections, details, schedules, symbols, dimensions, and notes. Candidates should practice moving between drawing sheets and understanding how the information relates to field construction.

Estimating should include basic dimensions, areas, volumes, quantities, and material takeoffs. Careful interpretation of drawings is important because an estimating mistake can begin with a simple measurement or plan-reading error.

The IBC, IRC, and ACI 318 should be used throughout preparation. Candidates should practice choosing the correct reference before beginning a lookup.

A useful exercise is to separate practice questions by reference at first. Work through a group of IBC questions, then IRC questions, then ACI 318 questions. Once the structure of each book becomes more familiar, mix the questions together.

Highlighted and tabbed books can support this process by providing an organized physical reference during study. Candidates should still learn how the books are structured so they can navigate beyond only the sections they have used most often.

Tables, definitions, chapter headings, and indexes should all receive attention. Many code questions require more than locating a section number; candidates must also read table headings, notes, exceptions, and limitations correctly.

Timed practice is important. With 80 questions in three hours, spending too long on one difficult code search can reduce the time available for easier questions. Candidates should practice moving forward and returning to difficult items when needed.

Appliance Installation, Sizing and Estimating, Testing and Inspection, and Combustion Air should not be overlooked. These subjects connect closely with the larger piping and venting categories and may require candidates to apply multiple concepts within one question.

The Nevada C-38 classification covers the specialty of installing equipment used with liquefied petroleum and natural gas. A contractor holding the full C-38 classification may perform work authorized under its related subclassifications.

The Gas Appliances and Equipment portion includes installation of appliances and equipment that require connection to a supply of liquefied petroleum or natural gas.

The Heating and Ventilating portion includes fabrication and installation of systems used to heat air with liquefied petroleum or natural gas and circulate that heated air.

Exam Details

The Nevada C-37A Solar Water Heating Contractor examination contains 45 questions. Candidates are allowed 1.5 hours to complete the examination and must answer 32 questions correctly to pass.

The examination content includes the following subject areas:

  • Piping
  • System Design
  • Pumps and Storage Systems
  • Collectors
  • System Valves and Controls
  • Safety

Candidates should prepare for a combination of code-based plumbing questions and practical solar thermal questions. The Uniform Plumbing Code is particularly useful for piping, materials, water-system provisions, fittings, supports, valves, and related installation requirements.

System-design questions require candidates to understand how solar collectors, piping, circulation, storage tanks, pumps, controls, and heat-transfer components work together to provide heated potable water.

Collectors, pumps, storage, valves, and controls should not be studied in isolation. Each component affects system operation, and exam questions may require candidates to understand relationships among several parts of the system.

With 45 questions in 1.5 hours, candidates have approximately two minutes per question on average. Efficient reference use and strong retained trade knowledge are both important for maintaining that pace.

Open Book Test

The Nevada C-37A Solar Water Heating Contractor examination is an open-book test.

The reference included in this package that is allowed into the trade examination is:

  • Uniform Plumbing Code, 2018

The following references are included for study but are not allowed into the trade examination room:

  • Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR Part 1926 (OSHA)
  • Solar Water and Pool Heating Design and Installation Manual

Candidates should use the Uniform Plumbing Code regularly throughout preparation. Become familiar with the table of contents, index, definitions, chapter organization, tables, exceptions, and cross-references.

Open-book testing is most effective when candidates already understand how the code is organized. Searching the entire book for every question can use too much time, especially when the average pace is approximately two minutes per question.

For questions involving piping materials, fittings, supports, valves, potable water, or connections, identify the technical subject first and then use the index or table of contents to narrow the search.

Questions involving collector operation, solar thermal system design, storage, pumps, controls, or jobsite safety may rely more heavily on knowledge developed before test day.

Nevada identifies C-37A as the Water Heating subclassification under the broader C-37 Solar Contractor classification.

The C-37A scope covers the installation of systems for the collection of solar energy to heat water for potable uses.

The classification does not authorize installation of pipes or fixtures other than water heaters and storage tanks designed for the use of the water so heated. Candidates should understand this scope limitation when studying for the trade examination and when evaluating the type of work authorized by the classification.

C-37A work can involve solar collectors, circulation piping, pumps, storage tanks, heat exchangers, valves, controls, insulation, and related components used to collect and transfer solar energy into potable water heating systems.

Because the classification involves potable water, plumbing-code knowledge is especially important. Candidates should be comfortable working with applicable Uniform Plumbing Code provisions involving materials, water systems, piping, fittings, supports, valves, and connections.

Test Information and Study Materials

A strong Nevada C-37A preparation plan should begin with complete solar water heating system design. Candidates should understand how solar collectors, piping, pumps, storage tanks, heat exchangers, valves, and controls operate together rather than treating each component as an isolated subject.

Follow the movement of thermal energy through the system. Understand how solar energy is captured at the collector, transferred into water or another working medium, circulated through piping, stored when necessary, and ultimately used to provide heated potable water.

Piping should receive substantial attention. Review pipe materials, fittings, joining methods, supports, routing, insulation, thermal expansion, valves, and connections.

The Uniform Plumbing Code, 2018 should be used throughout preparation rather than only during the final days before the exam. Repeated use helps candidates become more familiar with how the code is organized.

Practice locating code requirements by topic. Begin with a question involving pipe material, identify the key term, use the index, and locate the corresponding section. Repeat the same process with fittings, supports, valves, water heaters, storage tanks, and potable water provisions.

Definitions can be important because plumbing terminology may have a specific code meaning. Understanding the definition can help determine which requirement applies to an installation.

Tables should receive regular attention. Important requirements involving materials, supports, sizing, or installation conditions may appear in table format.

Exceptions can modify a general requirement. Candidates should read the surrounding code language carefully before selecting an answer.

Cross-references may direct the candidate to another section containing additional requirements. Practice following them instead of assuming the first section contains the complete answer.

Collectors are a core solar water heating component. Candidates should understand collector function, arrangement, mounting concepts, orientation, circulation, and how collectors transfer solar energy into the working fluid.

Review how collector configuration affects flow and how multiple collectors can operate as part of a larger thermal system.

Pumps should be studied in relation to circulation. Candidates should understand why pumps are used, how they move fluid through collectors and storage systems, and how improper circulation can affect performance.

Storage tanks are specifically important in solar water heating because solar energy availability and hot-water demand do not always occur at the same time. Candidates should understand how storage supports system operation.

Heat exchangers may be used to transfer thermal energy between separate fluid circuits. Candidates should understand their purpose and the basic relationship between the collector loop and potable water.

System Valves and Controls should include shutoff valves, check valves, balancing devices, temperature controls, differential controls, and other components used to regulate operation and circulation.

Safety preparation should include roof access, ladders, elevated work, personal protective equipment, tools, material handling, hot surfaces, electrical control components, and other construction hazards.

The Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR Part 1926 (OSHA) should be used during preparation to build retained safety knowledge because it is not allowed into the trade examination room.

The Solar Water and Pool Heating Design and Installation Manual can help connect multiple C-37A exam topics. Use it to review collector layouts, piping configurations, pumps, storage, controls, valves, circulation, heat-transfer concepts, and complete system operation.

Because this manual is not allowed into the exam room, active recall is useful. After reviewing a system diagram, close the book and explain the flow path and purpose of each major component from memory.

Potable water considerations should receive careful attention because the C-37A classification specifically covers systems used to heat water for potable uses.

Candidates should understand the relationship between the solar thermal system and the water-heating and storage components authorized by the classification.

Heat transfer is central to solar water heating. Understand how solar radiation becomes usable thermal energy and how that energy moves from the collector into the water-heating system.

Freeze protection can be important because collectors and piping may be exposed to outdoor temperatures. Candidates should understand general methods used to protect solar thermal components from damaging conditions.

Insulation helps reduce unwanted heat loss between the collector, storage system, and final water-heating application. Candidates should understand why solar thermal piping is insulated and how outdoor exposure affects system performance.

Thermal expansion should also be considered in systems exposed to elevated temperatures. Pipe movement, materials, supports, and system design can all affect installation.

A useful study schedule should divide preparation among Piping, System Design, Pumps and Storage Systems, Collectors, System Valves and Controls, and Safety.

Once individual subjects become familiar, move into mixed-question practice. The actual examination can shift quickly from a piping requirement to a collector question, storage issue, control topic, or safety scenario.

Timed UPC lookup drills can improve open-book performance. Choose a plumbing topic and practice locating the applicable requirement within a limited amount of time.

Do not expect the Uniform Plumbing Code to answer every question. The UPC is most useful for targeted code requirements, while many practical solar water heating questions require retained technical knowledge.

When a practice question is missed, identify the reason. The issue may involve weak trade knowledge, unfamiliar terminology, slow reference navigation, or difficulty understanding the relationship between multiple system components.

Correcting the underlying weakness is more useful than memorizing one answer. This approach builds stronger preparation for unfamiliar questions on test day.

Test Information and Study Materials

A productive Nevada C-21D study plan should focus heavily on troubleshooting and maintenance. The classification is built around repairing and replacing components in existing systems, so candidates should be able to evaluate symptoms and connect them to likely equipment or system problems.

The Refrigeration Cycle should be one of the first areas reviewed. Candidates should understand compression, condensation, expansion, and evaporation and how pressure, temperature, and refrigerant condition change throughout the cycle.

Compressors are central to refrigeration and air-conditioning systems. Review compressor function, operating conditions, electrical components, lubrication concepts, overheating, abnormal pressures, and common causes of compressor failure.

Condensers should be studied in relation to heat rejection, airflow, coil condition, fan operation, ambient temperature, and pressure. Candidates should understand how restricted airflow or dirty surfaces can affect system performance.

Evaporators should be reviewed in relation to heat absorption, airflow, coil temperature, refrigerant condition, icing, and drainage. Problems in the evaporator section can produce symptoms that resemble refrigerant or airflow issues.

Metering Devices should be studied according to their role in controlling refrigerant flow and creating the pressure difference needed for the refrigeration cycle. Candidates should understand how improper operation can affect superheat, evaporator performance, and system pressures.

Refrigerant System Troubleshooting should include recognition of abnormal high-side and low-side pressures, undercharge, overcharge, airflow restrictions, refrigerant restrictions, contamination, and component problems.

Controls and Electrical Components are another major part of maintenance work. Candidates should review relays, contactors, thermostats, capacitors, motors, pressure switches, transformers, safety controls, and basic control circuits.

A technician should understand how to separate an electrical failure from a refrigeration-system failure. A compressor that does not run, for example, can result from control issues, electrical problems, safety-device operation, or compressor failure.

Motors and Blowers should be studied in relation to airflow, electrical operation, rotation, bearings, capacitors, speed, and mechanical condition. Poor airflow can affect both comfort and refrigeration-system pressures.

Heat Exchangers and heating components should be reviewed where they are part of existing HVAC systems. Candidates should understand basic operating principles, inspection concerns, airflow effects, and maintenance considerations.

Piping and Tubing should include refrigerant line function, fittings, supports, insulation, leaks, restrictions, and proper service practices. The condition of piping can affect pressure drop, refrigerant flow, oil return, and overall system performance.

System Testing should include pressure and temperature evaluation, electrical measurements, airflow observations, leak detection concepts, and the process of comparing actual system behavior with expected operation.

Preventive Maintenance should be considered alongside repair work. Cleaning coils, checking filters, inspecting electrical connections, evaluating motors, examining condensate systems, and monitoring system operation can help identify issues before larger failures occur.

The Troubleshooting and Servicing Modern Air Conditioning and Refrigeration Systems reference should be used to develop a systematic diagnostic approach. The Uniform Mechanical Code, 2018 should be handled differently because it is permitted during the exam. Practice using the table of contents, index, definitions, refrigeration chapters, equipment provisions, and ventilation sections under timed conditions.

A useful study method is to work through troubleshooting questions without the technical books nearby, then use the UMC only when the question requires a specific mechanical code provision. This better reflects the balance between retained technical knowledge and open-book navigation.

Time management should also be practiced. With 60 questions in two hours, candidates should avoid spending several minutes searching for one answer. If a lookup becomes difficult, continue with the exam and return later when possible.

Reinforcement should receive dedicated attention. Structural masonry can use reinforcing steel, anchors, ties, and related components to improve performance and connect masonry to surrounding construction.

Stone Masonry should be studied for material selection, cutting, placement, bonding, support, and finishing. Stone work can differ substantially from standard concrete masonry or brick construction, so candidates should understand the basic trade principles involved.

Wall Layout and Construction should include dimensions, corners, openings, lines, levels, plumb conditions, coursing, and proper sequencing. Accurate layout is essential because small errors can compound as wall height increases.

Openings and Structural Features should include lintels, supports, reinforcement around openings, bearing conditions, and the way doors, windows, or other penetrations affect masonry systems.

Flashing and Moisture Control should be reviewed as part of wall performance. Candidates should understand how moisture can enter masonry construction and why proper detailing is important.

Structural Masonry Requirements should be practiced through ACI 530/530.1. Learn how the reference is organized and where requirements involving materials, reinforcement, structural walls, specifications, and construction quality can be found.

Building Code Requirements should be practiced through the International Building Code. Candidates should become familiar with the organization of the code and the relationship between general building requirements and masonry construction.

Masonry Tools and Equipment should include tools used for mixing, cutting, laying, aligning, measuring, striking joints, and handling masonry materials. Candidates should understand both the purpose and safe use of common equipment.

Scaffolds and Ladders are important safety subjects because masonry work frequently takes place above ground level. Review safe access, working platforms, fall hazards, and equipment conditions through OSHA study.

Material Handling deserves attention because masonry units, mortar materials, reinforcing steel, and equipment can be heavy. Safe storage, lifting, movement, and staging contribute to both productivity and jobsite safety.

Code-navigation practice should be timed. Choose a masonry question, identify the central subject, decide whether the International Building Code or ACI 530/530.1 is the better starting point, and then locate the requirement efficiently.

Nevada's C-1D Plumbing classification authorizes installation and maintenance of material and fixtures used to provide sanitary conditions in buildings through a permanent supply of safe water and sanitary waste and vent systems required for proper waste removal.

C-1D work includes a permanent means of supplying gas for residential and industrial purposes, along with piping for compressed air, vacuums, and gases used for medical purposes. The classification also permits applicable water and gas piping between the edge of a building and the utility meter.

Approved reference books may be highlighted, underlined, and indexed before the examination. Permanent tabs may be used. Temporary tabs are not permitted, and candidates should not add written notes or loose or attached papers to approved exam references.

Licensing Steps

  1. Confirm the C-1 classification. Make sure Nevada Plumbing and Heating Contracting matches the full scope of work the business intends to perform.
  2. Identify the qualifying individual. The contractor application must designate the person responsible for meeting the applicable trade qualification requirements.
  3. Document qualifying experience. Prepare the required experience information for the classification.
  4. Submit the Nevada contractor license application. Complete the applicable application and supporting documentation.
  5. Receive examination eligibility. After qualification information is reviewed, the qualifying individual can proceed with the applicable examinations.
  6. Prepare for the C-1 trade examination. Study plumbing, mechanical systems, boilers, fire sprinklers, hydronics, gas, chilled-water piping, industrial piping, safety, and related topics.
  7. Practice reference navigation. Work regularly with the UPC, UMC, NFPA 13, NFPA 54, and NFPA 58.
  8. Prepare for Nevada Business and Law. Contractor applicants must also satisfy the applicable business and law examination requirement unless an authorized waiver applies.
  9. Complete the required examinations. Take the applicable trade and business examinations.
  10. Complete remaining licensing requirements. Finish the additional requirements associated with issuance of the Nevada contractor license.

State Requirements

Nevada's C-1 Plumbing and Heating Contracting classification is a broad specialty license. A person holding the primary C-1 classification may perform work authorized under the C-1 subclassifications.

The scope includes boilers and hot-water or steam piping with related fittings, valves, gauges, pumps, radiators, tanks, fuel-oil lines, chimneys, flues, and associated work. It also includes fire sprinkler systems and insulation of pipes and ducts.

C-1 work also extends to plumbing systems providing safe water, sanitary waste and venting, roof drainage, hydronic heating systems within the applicable classification scope, landscape irrigation, potable-water heating systems including solar equipment, and gas supply systems.

The classification further reaches into sheet metal fabrication and installation, heating and evaporative cooling systems, gas pipes and vents, water heaters, chilled-water piping, firefighter breathing-air systems, and industrial piping used to transport water, steam, gas, chemicals, food, and other substances.

Because the primary C-1 classification covers such a wide range of work, the examination is considerably broader than a plumbing-only test. Candidates should prepare for both plumbing and mechanical construction along with specialized subjects such as fire sprinklers, industrial piping, hydronics, refrigeration-related systems, welding, and safety.

Test Information and Study Materials

A productive Nevada C-1 study plan should divide preparation into major systems rather than attempting to read every reference from beginning to end.

Drain, Waste, and Vent Systems should receive substantial attention. Review drainage sizing, slope, vents, fixture units, cleanouts, traps, interceptors, and sanitary-system requirements using the Uniform Plumbing Code.

Water Supply preparation should include sizing, pressure, materials, valves, backflow protection, supports, distribution, and system protection. Candidates should practice locating applicable UPC tables quickly.

Gas Systems should be studied with NFPA 54 and NFPA 58. Learn how natural gas and LP-Gas systems differ and practice selecting the correct reference before beginning a lookup.

Fire Sprinklers should be studied with NFPA 13. Focus on sprinkler systems, piping, components, spacing concepts, and installation requirements relevant to the C-1 examination.

Hydronics and Boilers should include heating-system components, pumps, valves, piping, heat transfer, controls, and boiler-related knowledge. The UMC and Modern Hydronic Heating reference can be used together during preparation.

Chilled Water Piping accounts for 6 questions. Candidates should review piping materials, valves, pumps, supports, insulation considerations, and system-operation concepts associated with chilled-water distribution.

Plumbing Mathematics and Isometric Analysis accounts for 8 questions. Practice pipe calculations, dimensions, elevations, geometry, offsets, areas, volumes, and plan interpretation until the steps become familiar.

Industrial Piping should include system materials, valves, equipment, supports, joining methods, and piping used for water, steam, gas, chemicals, food, and other industrial substances.

Safety should be learned before test day because the OSHA reference is not allowed into the examination. Use the study reference to strengthen knowledge of jobsite hazards, protective equipment, tools, excavation, and general construction safety.

Welding knowledge can support industrial and mechanical piping preparation. Review joint preparation, welding methods, equipment, workmanship, and safe procedures using Modern Welding.

Heating, Cooling, and Refrigeration concepts should also be part of the study plan because the C-1 classification includes heating and air-circulation work. Modern Refrigeration and Air Conditioning can support this broader mechanical review.

Choose a question, identify whether it belongs in the UPC, UMC, NFPA 13, NFPA 54, or NFPA 58, and then locate the applicable provision. The ability to choose the correct book quickly can save as much time as knowing how to use the index.

With 120 questions in five hours, pacing matters. Candidates should avoid spending excessive time on one code lookup. If a question is taking too long, move forward and return later if time remains.

Exam Details

The Nevada B General Building Contractor examination contains 80 questions. Candidates are allowed 3 hours to complete the examination, and the minimum passing score is 56 correct answers.

The examination covers a broad range of general building subjects, including:

  • Sitework
  • Concrete
  • Masonry
  • Metals
  • Carpentry
  • Thermal and Moisture Protection
  • Doors and Windows
  • Drywall and Finishes
  • Safety
  • General Code, Plan Reading, and Estimating
  • Nevada One Call

Because the exam covers multiple construction trades, candidates should avoid concentrating exclusively on one area such as concrete or framing. General Building contractors are expected to understand how building systems are coordinated and how construction activities affect one another throughout a project.

With 80 questions and three hours available, candidates have an average of approximately two minutes and fifteen seconds per question. Efficient decision-making is important. Code references should be used strategically when detailed confirmation is needed, while straightforward trade questions should be answered from existing knowledge when possible.

Plan reading and estimating also require practical preparation. Candidates should be comfortable interpreting dimensions, construction details, symbols, building systems, material quantities, and common construction calculations.

Licensing Steps

The Nevada B General Building examination is one component of the Nevada contractor licensing process. Applicants must complete the applicable licensing requirements in addition to preparing for the trade examination.

  1. Confirm the General Building classification. Determine that the proposed contracting work falls within Nevada's Classification B scope.
  2. Identify the qualifying individual. The contractor application must designate the individual who provides the required experience and trade qualification.
  3. Prepare qualifying experience documentation. The qualifying individual should document applicable general building experience involving the construction or remodeling of buildings and coordination of multiple trades.
  4. Complete the contractor license application. Submit the required business, qualifying individual, financial, experience, and supporting information.
  5. Submit the application for review. The Nevada State Contractors Board reviews the application before examination eligibility is established.
  6. Receive examination eligibility. Once approved to test, the qualifying individual can proceed with scheduling the required examinations.
  7. Prepare for the B General Building examination. Study the major building trades and practice using the approved exam-room references.
  8. Complete applicable examinations. Candidates must satisfy the General Building trade examination and the Nevada Contractor Management Survey requirements unless an applicable waiver is approved.
  9. Complete remaining licensing requirements. All other applicable licensing requirements must be satisfied before the contractor license is issued.

Nevada also recognizes certain pathways that can affect the trade examination requirement, including approved licensure by endorsement and the NASCLA Accredited Examination for qualifying General Building applicants. Those pathways do not remove the other applicable Nevada licensing requirements.

State Requirements

Nevada defines a Classification B General Building Contractor as a contractor whose principal business involves construction or remodeling of buildings or structures intended to support, shelter, or enclose persons, animals, chattels, or other movable property.

A General Building project must require the use of more than two unrelated building trades or crafts, with the General Building contractor serving as the prime contractor and with construction or remodeling of the building as the project's primary purpose.

The General Building classification does not automatically authorize a contractor to self-perform every specialty trade. Plumbing, electrical, refrigeration and air conditioning, and fire protection work require the appropriate specialty license when the General Building contractor intends to perform that work directly.

Qualifying experience for a Nevada contractor license generally requires four full years of applicable experience within the 15 years immediately preceding the application. The experience must relate to the classification being requested and satisfy the applicable Nevada licensing standards.

Applicants should make sure their work history demonstrates genuine general building experience rather than experience limited to a single specialty trade. The B classification is centered on building construction and the coordination of multiple unrelated trades.

Test Information and Study Materials

A strong Nevada General Building study plan should divide preparation among the major construction trades instead of reading every reference from beginning to end without a clear structure.

Sitework should include excavation, grading, trenching, underground utilities, site preparation, backfill, compaction, and construction coordination. Pipe and Excavation Contracting and the Nevada One Call materials support these subjects.

Concrete requires both code knowledge and practical construction understanding. Use ACI 318 for structural requirements and The Contractor's Guide to Quality Concrete Construction for practical material handling, placement, consolidation, finishing, curing, and quality concepts.

Masonry should include structural code provisions as well as field practices. ACI 530/530.1 supports structural masonry requirements, while Modern Masonry reinforces practical construction methods, mortar, units, layout, tools, and workmanship.

Metals should include structural steel-related concepts and safe handling of joists and joist girders. The steel joist technical digest can help candidates understand erection procedures and stability considerations before test day.

Carpentry preparation should include framing concepts, structural components, layout, building systems, openings, and coordination with other trades. Candidates should also understand how carpentry relates to code requirements in the International Building Code.

Thermal and Moisture Protection should include building-envelope concepts, insulation, roofing, flashing, moisture control, waterproofing, and related construction practices.

Doors and Windows should be reviewed for installation, openings, hardware, dimensions, code considerations, and coordination with wall systems and finishes.

Drywall and Finishes should include gypsum board systems, framing, fasteners, joints, finishing, assemblies, and related installation methods. The Gypsum Construction Handbook is especially useful for pre-exam study in this area.

Safety should receive regular attention through OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926. Because that book is not permitted in the examination room, candidates should learn major construction safety concepts before testing rather than relying on reference searches.

Plan Reading and Estimating should be practiced with actual construction-style problems. Review dimensions, scales, symbols, material quantities, square footage, cubic measurements, elevations, details, and coordination between plans and specifications.

Post-tensioning should be reviewed through the included Level 1 field fundamentals material. Understand terminology, tendon placement, anchorage, field handling, stressing concepts, and safety considerations.

For the open-book portion of preparation, practice timed navigation with the International Building Code, ACI 318, and ACI 530/530.1. Choose a subject, identify the likely reference, locate the applicable provision, and review the surrounding language.

For study-only references, use active recall. Study a topic, close the book, answer practice questions, and return to the reference afterward to correct mistakes. This helps prepare candidates for questions that cannot be answered through an exam-room lookup.

A balanced study routine should combine code navigation, practical construction knowledge, calculations, safety review, plan reading, and trade-specific practice. General Building candidates need breadth as well as depth because the examination spans many unrelated construction crafts.

The Nevada A-19 Pipeline and Conduits examination contains 60 questions. Candidates are allowed 2 hours to complete the examination and must answer 42 questions correctly to pass.

The examination content is divided into the following areas:

  • Gas Piping: 15 questions
  • Water Piping: 15 questions
  • Welding: 6 questions
  • Safety: 8 questions
  • Paving: 5 questions
  • Excavation, Compaction and Grading: 8 questions
  • Nevada One Call: 3 questions

Gas Piping and Water Piping together make up half of the examination. Candidates should understand pipeline materials, fittings, installation procedures, joining methods, protection, testing concepts, trench conditions, and the differences between systems intended for water and gas service.

Safety and Excavation, Compaction and Grading each account for 8 questions. Underground construction introduces hazards involving trenches, heavy equipment, buried utilities, moving vehicles, material handling, and changing soil conditions. Candidates should treat these subjects as core A-19 knowledge.

Welding accounts for 6 questions. Preparation should include pipe preparation, welding procedures, joints, equipment, workmanship, and concepts related to producing suitable welded connections.

Paving accounts for 5 questions because pipeline projects frequently require restoration of streets, driveways, or other paved surfaces after trenching and underground work are completed.

The Nevada A-19 Pipeline and Conduits examination is an open-book test.

  6. Prepare for the A-19 examination. Study gas piping, water piping, welding, excavation, grading, compaction, safety, paving, and Nevada One Call.
